RULE 8: While a WRS.STO stall is in progress, the stall MUST continue only while the implementation-defined short timeout has not yet elapsed.
RULE 9: While a WRS.STO stall is in progress, the stall MUST continue only while no pending interrupt is observed.
RULE 10: If a pending interrupt becomes observed during a WRS.STO stall, the stall MUST end and execution must resume according to the same rules that apply to the WFI instruction.

INSTRUCTION: XNOR
FORMAT: xnor rd, rs1, rs2
RULE 1: XNOR must compute the bitwise NOT of the XOR of the values in rs1 and rs2 and write the resulting XLEN-wide value to rd.
RULE 2: XNOR is defined for both RV32 and RV64 base ISA extensions, so it operates on 32-bit values in RV32 and on 64-bit values in RV64.
RULE 3: XNOR reads the integer registers specified as rs1 and rs2 and writes the computed result to the integer register specified as rd.
RULE 4: An implementation that supports the Zbkb extension must provide the XNOR instruction.
RULE 5: The XNOR instruction must be present in RV32 implementations that include the Zbkb extension.
RULE 6: The XNOR instruction must be present in RV64 implementations that include the Zbkb extension.
RULE 7: The XNOR instruction performs a bitwise exclusive-NOR operation on its two source operands and writes the resulting value to the destination register.
RULE 8: The vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction computes each mask element i as the logical NOT of the exclusive-OR of the corresponding bits of vs2.mask[i] and vs1.mask[i], i.e., vd.mask[i] = !(vs2.mask[i] ^^ vs1.mask[i]).
RULE 9: The vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction operates only on mask registers, where each element is a single-bit mask value.
RULE 10: The destination vector register of the vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction may be the same physical register as either source vector register.
RULE 11: During execution of the vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction, mask elements whose indices are less than the current vstart value remain unchanged.
RULE 12: After the vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction completes, the architectural vstart register is reset to zero.
RULE 13: All vmxnor.mm XNOR executions are unmasked, meaning no element is considered inactive regardless of the vm field.
RULE 14: Encodings of the vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction with the vm field equal to zero are reserved and have undefined architectural behavior.
RULE 15: The vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction updates mask elements whose indices are greater than or equal to vl according to the tail-agnostic policy defined for vector mask logical instructions.
RULE 16: The vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction always uses a single vector register for its operation irrespective of the vlmul setting in the vtype register.
RULE 17: Execution of the vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction does not modify the architectural vlmul field.
RULE 18: The assembler pseudoinstruction vmset.m, which expands to vmxnor.mm XNOR vd, vd, vd, sets every mask element in vd to logical one.
RULE 19: The logical function performed by vmxnor.mm XNOR corresponds to the truth-table pattern 1 0 0 1, representing the XNOR of the two input mask bits.
RULE 20: When the vmxnor.mm XNOR instruction is used with identical source and destination registers (vd, vd, vd), the result is a mask register whose every element is set to one.
RULE 21: The XNOR instruction computes a bit-wise exclusive-NOR of the architectural values in rs1 and rs2, producing a result where each bit is 1 if the corresponding bits of rs1 and rs2 are equal and 0 otherwise.
RULE 22: The XNOR instruction writes the computed bit-wise exclusive-NOR result into the destination register rd.
RULE 23: The XNOR instruction reads the architectural values of source registers rs1 and rs2 without modifying either register.
RULE 24: The XNOR instruction MUST be implemented in RV32 base ISA implementations.
RULE 25: The XNOR instruction MUST be implemented in RV64 base ISA implementations.
RULE 26: The XNOR instruction is defined as performing a bitwise exclusive-NOR of its two source registers and writing the result to the destination register.
RULE 27: The vmxnor XNOR instruction is encoded with the funct6 field set to the binary value 011111.

INSTRUCTION: XOR
FORMAT: xor rd, rs1, rs2
RULE 1: The XORI instruction is an integer register-immediate operation that must compute a bitwise XOR between the value in source register rs1 and a 12-bit immediate.
RULE 2: The 12-bit immediate used by an XORI instruction must be sign-extended to XLEN bits before the XOR operation is performed.
RULE 3: The result of the XOR between the sign-extended immediate and the value in rs1 must be written to the destination register rd.
RULE 4: If the immediate field of an XORI instruction is –1, the sign-extended immediate consists of all 1 bits, causing the XOR to produce the bitwise logical inversion of rs1 and store the result in rd, which is equivalent to the NOT pseudoinstruction.
RULE 5: XOR MUST read the contents of registers rs1 and rs2 as source operands and MUST write the computed result into register rd.
RULE 6: XOR MUST compute a bitwise logical exclusive-OR of each pair of corresponding bits of rs1 and rs2, producing an XLEN-wide result that is written to rd.
RULE 7: If register rc equals zero, the conditional XOR operation must write to rd the result of the bitwise exclusive-or of rs1 and rs2.
RULE 8: If register rc does not equal zero, the conditional XOR operation must write to rd the result of the bitwise exclusive-or of rs1 and rs2.
RULE 9: An AMOXOR instruction must atomically load a data value from the address in rs1, place the loaded value into rd, compute the bitwise XOR of the loaded value and the original value in rs2, and store the XOR result back to the same address in rs1.
RULE 10: When an AMOXOR instruction operates on a 32-bit word in RV64, the 32-bit XOR result placed in rd must be sign-extended to 64 bits and the upper 32 bits of rs2 must be ignored.
RULE 11: If the address in rs1 for an AMOXOR instruction is not naturally aligned to the operand size, the implementation must raise either an address-misaligned exception or an access-fault exception.
RULE 12: If a misaligned atomicity granule PMA is defined and all bytes accessed by an AMOXOR instruction lie within the same granule, the instruction must not raise an alignment exception and must perform a single atomic memory operation.
RULE 13: When the aq bit is set on an AMOXOR instruction, no later memory operations in the same hart may be observed to occur before the AMOXOR.
RULE 14: When the rl bit is set on an AMOXOR instruction, other harts must not observe the AMOXOR before any memory accesses that precede it in the same hart.
RULE 15: When both aq and rl bits are set on an AMOXOR instruction, the operation is sequentially consistent, meaning it cannot be reordered with earlier or later memory operations from the same hart.
RULE 16: AMOXOR.B/H must sign-extend the original memory value placed into rd after performing the XOR operation, extending it to the processor's XLEN.
RULE 17: AMOXOR.B/H must ignore any bits of rs2 that lie outside the operand width when computing the XOR result.
RULE 18: AMOXOR.B/H must use an address in rs1 that is naturally aligned to the operand size; if the address is not naturally aligned, the instruction triggers the misaligned-address exception defined for atomic instructions.
RULE 19: AMOXOR.B/H must apply the same exception behavior as specified for atomic instructions in the base A extension when an exception condition occurs.
RULE 20: AMOXOR.B/H may set the aq and rl bits to provide optional acquire and release ordering semantics for the XOR operation, following the release-consistency rules for atomic memory operations.
RULE 21: AMOXOR.B/H uses the width field to select the operand size, where width=0 causes the XOR operation to act on a byte and width=1 causes it to act on a halfword.
RULE 22: The c.not instruction MUST compute the value of the architectural register X(rsdc) as X(rsdc) XOR 1 and write the result back to the same register.
RULE 23: The XORI instruction with immediate –1 MUST compute the bitwise exclusive-or of the source register rd'/rs1' with the constant value –1 (all bits set) and write the result to the destination register rd'.
RULE 24: The XORI instruction with immediate –1 MUST provide the 32-bit equivalent behavior of the c.not instruction.
RULE 25: When the immediate field imm of the vxor.vi (vector-immediate) form of the XOR instruction is set to -1, the instruction performs a bitwise NOT operation on the source vector.
RULE 26: The assembler pseudoinstruction vnot.v vd,vs,vm is defined to expand to the XOR instruction form vxor.vi vd,vs,-1,vm.
RULE 27: The vector reduction XOR instruction (vredxor.vs) MUST use the same SEW width for all source operands and for the destination register.
RULE 28: The vector reduction XOR instruction (vredxor.vs) computes vd[0] as the bitwise XOR of vs1[0] with the bitwise XOR of all active elements of vs2.
RULE 29: The vmxor.mm XOR operation sets each destination mask bit to the exclusive-OR of the corresponding source mask bits from the two source vector registers.
RULE 30: The vmxor.mm XOR instruction operates on mask registers where each element is a single bit, and it always uses a single vector register regardless of the vlmul field in vtype.
RULE 31: The destination register of the vmxor.mm XOR instruction may be the same register as either source operand.
RULE 32: For the vmxor.mm XOR instruction, mask elements whose indices are less than the current vstart value remain unchanged, and the vstart field is reset to zero after the instruction completes.
RULE 33: The vmxor.mm XOR instruction is always unmasked, meaning no elements are considered inactive, and any encoding with vm=0 is reserved.
RULE 34: The vmxor.mm XOR instruction updates mask elements whose indices are greater than or equal to the current vector length (vl) according to the tail-agnostic policy, regardless of the tail status.
RULE 35: Executing vmxor.mm XOR with both source operands equal to the destination register (vd, vd, vd) produces a mask register whose every element is zero, effectively clearing the register.
RULE 36: The vmxor.mm XOR instruction implements the logical truth table where 0 XOR 0 yields 0, 0 XOR 1 yields 1, 1 XOR 0 yields 1, and 1 XOR 1 yields 0 for each mask element.
RULE 37: The XOR operation of this instruction must compute a bitwise exclusive-OR between the 128-bit round-key element and each 128-bit element group of the destination register vd, producing a new 128-bit element group for each group.
RULE 38: After execution, each element group of the destination register vd must contain the result of XORing the corresponding original element group with the round key.
RULE 39: The .vv form of this instruction must produce identical architectural results to the vxor.vv vd, vs2, vd instruction.
RULE 40: The XOR performed by the .vv form must therefore exhibit the same architectural behavior as the XOR performed by this instruction.
RULE 41: The implementation of this XOR instruction must guarantee that its execution latency does not depend on the operand data values.
RULE 42: The XOR operation of the vxor.vv instruction must also have execution latency independent of the operand data values.
RULE 43: The AMOLogical support level indicates that swap instructions and all logical AMOs—including amoand, amoor, and amoxor (XOR)—are supported.
RULE 44: A naturally aligned amoxor (XOR) of a given width is architecturally supported only when the accessed memory region permits reads and writes of that width.
RULE 45: A memory region may not support the amoxor (XOR) operation even if the processor implements amoxor, making the instruction unavailable for that region.

INSTRUCTION: XORI
FORMAT: xori rd, rs1, imm12
RULE 1: XORI must compute the bitwise exclusive-OR of the value in integer register rs1 and the sign-extended 12-bit immediate, and must write the resulting XLEN-bit value into integer register rd.
RULE 2: XORI must sign-extend the 12-bit immediate operand to the processor's XLEN width before the exclusive-OR operation is performed.
RULE 3: XORI with an immediate value of –1 must produce a result equal to the bitwise logical inversion of the value in rs1 and must place that inverted value into rd, which is equivalent to the NOT pseudoinstruction.
RULE 4: An XORI instruction whose destination register equals its source register and whose immediate operand is -1 functions as the 32-bit equivalent of the compressed c.not instruction.
RULE 5: When an XORI instruction has its destination register identical to its source register and its immediate operand is -1, the instruction computes the bitwise NOT of the original register value and writes that result back to the same register.

INSTRUCTION: XPERM4
FORMAT: xperm4 rd, rs1, rs2
RULE 1: XPERM4 implements a lookup-table permutation operation on 4-bit (nibble) elements stored in general-purpose registers.
RULE 2: XPERM4 may also be used to permute 8-bit elements within registers as a lookup-table operation.
RULE 3: In an XPERM4 execution the source register rs1 is interpreted as a vector of N-bit words, where N is the element size selected for the permutation.
RULE 4: In an XPERM4 execution the source register rs2 is interpreted as a vector of N-bit indices that select elements from the rs1 vector.
RULE 5: For each N-bit element position, XPERM4 obtains the index from the corresponding N-bit element of rs2; if the index is less than the number of N-bit elements present in rs1, XPERM4 writes to the destination register the N-bit element from rs1 at that index, otherwise XPERM4 writes zero for that element.
RULE 6: XPERM4 writes the resulting vector of N-bit elements, each selected or zero-filled as specified, into the destination register rd.
RULE 7: XPERM4 MUST interpret the source register rs1 as a vector of XLEN/4 consecutive 4-bit elements (nibbles) and the source register rs2 as a vector of XLEN/4 consecutive 4-bit indexes.
RULE 8: XPERM4 MUST, for each multiple-of-4 bit position i from 0 to XLEN-4, extract the 4-bit index from rs2 bits i+3 down to i.
RULE 9: XPERM4 MUST replace the extracted index nibble with the 4-bit element from rs1 whose nibble position equals the index value, provided the index value is less than XLEN/4.
RULE 10: XPERM4 MUST produce a zero nibble in the destination position when the extracted index value is greater than or equal to XLEN/4.
RULE 11: XPERM4 MUST assemble the destination register rd by placing each resulting 4-bit element (or zero) into the corresponding nibble position i+3..i for all i that are multiples of 4 across the XLEN-bit width.
RULE 12: XPERM4 MUST initialize the result vector to all zeros before processing any nibbles, so that any nibble not written by a lookup remains zero.
RULE 13: XPERM4 MUST write the final XLEN-bit result into rd and retire successfully.
RULE 14: XPERM4 MUST place into bits i+3 down to i of the result the low-order 4 bits of rs1 after right-shifting rs1 by (idx × 4) bits, where idx is the 4-bit index extracted from rs2 for that nibble.
RULE 15: XPERM4 MUST write zero into bits i+3 down to i of the result when the extracted idx value multiplied by 4 is greater than or equal to XLEN (i.e., the index is out of bounds).
RULE 16: XPERM4 MUST write the assembled result to rd after all nibbles have been processed.
RULE 17: XPERM4 operates on 4-bit elements (nibbles) of the source registers.
RULE 18: XPERM4 treats the value in rs1 as a vector of XLEN/4 unsigned 4-bit elements.
RULE 19: XPERM4 treats the value in rs2 as a vector of XLEN/4 unsigned 4-bit index elements.
RULE 20: XPERM4 produces a result in rd where each 4-bit element is the 4-bit element of rs1 indexed by the corresponding 4-bit element of rs2, or zero if that index is out of bounds.

INSTRUCTION: XPERM8
FORMAT: xperm8 rd, rs1, rs2
RULE 1: An RV32 or RV64 implementation MUST support the XPERM8 instruction.
RULE 2: The XPERM8 instruction treats each byte of source register rs1 as an independent 8-bit table entry.
RULE 3: The XPERM8 instruction treats each byte of source register rs2 as an 8-bit index into the byte vector of rs1.
RULE 4: For each byte position i, the XPERM8 instruction selects the byte from rs1 whose index equals the i-th byte of rs2 and writes that selected byte to the i-th byte position of rd.
RULE 5: If the i-th byte of rs2 is greater than or equal to the number of bytes in rs1, the XPERM8 instruction writes a zero byte to the i-th byte position of rd.
RULE 6: XPERM8 treats the source register rs1 as a vector of XLEN/8 independent 8-bit elements.
RULE 7: XPERM8 treats the source register rs2 as a vector of XLEN/8 independent 8-bit index elements.
RULE 8: For each byte position i (0, 8, …, XLEN-8) XPERM8 replaces the result byte at that position with the 8-bit element of rs1 whose index equals the 8-bit value of rs2 at the same position, provided the index is less than XLEN/8.
RULE 9: If the 8-bit index taken from rs2 at a given byte position i is greater than or equal to XLEN/8, XPERM8 writes zero into the result byte at position i.
RULE 10: XPERM8 computes each result byte by shifting the full XLEN-bit value of rs1 right by (index × 8) bits and extracting the low 8 bits of the shifted value.
RULE 11: XPERM8 writes the concatenation of all result bytes into the destination register rd, with any bits not explicitly written remaining zero because the result is initially zero-extended.
RULE 12: XPERM8 completes execution without raising an architectural exception and retires successfully.
RULE 13: XPERM8 treats the source register rs1 as a vector of XLEN/8 consecutive 8-bit elements.
RULE 14: XPERM8 treats the source register rs2 as a vector of XLEN/8 consecutive 8-bit index elements.
RULE 15: XPERM8 initializes a temporary XLEN-bit result value to zero before processing any byte positions.
RULE 16: For each byte position i (where i = 0, 8, …, XLEN-8) XPERM8 reads the index byte from rs2 bits i+7 down to i.
RULE 17: XPERM8 selects a byte from rs1 by right-shifting rs1 by (index × 8) bits and extracting the least-significant 8 bits of the shifted value.
RULE 18: If the index byte read from rs2 is greater than or equal to XLEN/8, XPERM8 writes zero into the corresponding byte position of the destination register rd.
RULE 19: If the index byte read from rs2 is less than XLEN/8, XPERM8 writes the selected byte from rs1 into the corresponding byte position of rd.
RULE 20: XPERM8 writes each resulting byte into rd at the same byte position i from which the index was taken, forming the complete XLEN-bit destination value.
RULE 21: XPERM8 completes execution with a successful retirement and does not raise an exception for any defined index values.
RULE 22: XPERM8 performs a byte-wise crossbar permutation of the source operand bytes to produce its result.
RULE 23: XPERM8 is part of the Zbkb, Zbkc, and Zbkx extensions, so the instruction is available when any of those extensions are implemented.
RULE 24: XPERM8 treats the value in register rs1 as a vector of XLEN/8 independent 8-bit elements.
RULE 25: XPERM8 treats the value in register rs2 as a vector of XLEN/8 independent 8-bit index elements.
RULE 26: XPERM8 writes to each byte i of the destination register rd the byte from rs1 whose position equals the unsigned index value contained in byte i of rs2, provided that index value is less than XLEN/8.
RULE 27: XPERM8 writes zero to byte i of the destination register rd when the unsigned index value contained in byte i of rs2 is greater than or equal to XLEN/8.

INSTRUCTION: ZEXT.H
FORMAT: zext.h rd, rs1
RULE 1: An implementation that advertises support for the Zcb extension MUST provide the ZEXT.H instruction.
RULE 2: The ZEXT.H instruction (compressed form c.zext.h) zero-extends the low 16-bit halfword of the source register and writes the resulting value to the destination register rsd'.
RULE 3: ZEXT.H must take a single operand that is used as both the source and the destination register.
RULE 4: ZEXT.H must zero-extend the least-significant halfword (bits 15 down to 0) of the operand to XLEN bits by inserting zeros into all bits more significant than bit 15.
RULE 5: ZEXT.H must read and write a register whose architectural number is in the range x8-x15.
RULE 6: ZEXT.H is only defined when the Zbb extension is implemented; if Zbb is not present, the instruction is reserved/illegal.
RULE 7: ZEXT.H extracts the least-significant 16 bits of the source register rs.
RULE 8: ZEXT.H zero-extends the extracted 16-bit value to the processor's XLEN.
RULE 9: ZEXT.H writes the zero-extended XLEN-wide result to the destination register rd.
RULE 10: ZEXT.H produces an XLEN-wide result, which is 32 bits on RV32 and 64 bits on RV64.
RULE 11: ZEXT.H does not cause any architectural side effects other than updating rd.
RULE 12: ZEXT.H does not perform privilege checks or raise exceptions under normal operation.
RULE 13: ZEXT.H rd, rs must zero-extend the least-significant 16 bits of the source register rs and write the resulting XLEN-bit value into the destination register rd.
RULE 14: The architectural effect of ZEXT.H rd, rs is identical to the effect of executing the instruction sequence slli rd, rs, 16 followed by srli rd, rd, 16.
RULE 15: ZEXT.H is defined and must be available in implementations of both the RV32 and RV64 base ISAs.
RULE 16: When rs2 = x0, ZEXT.H copies the low XLEN/2 bits of rs1 into the low half of rd and zero-extends them to XLEN.
RULE 17: The ZEXT.H instruction packs the low 16 bits of rs1 and the low 16 bits of rs2 (which is zero) into the low 32 bits of rd.
RULE 18: The ZEXT.H instruction places the low 16 bits of rs1 into bits [15:0] of rd.
RULE 19: The ZEXT.H instruction sets bits [31:16] of rd to zero because rs2 is x0.
RULE 20: The ZEXT.H instruction sign-extends the resulting 32-bit value to the full XLEN of the destination register.
RULE 21: Because the 32-bit value produced by ZEXT.H has bit 31 equal to zero, the sign-extension performed by ZEXT.H leaves all bits above bit 31 in rd equal to zero.
RULE 22: ZEXT.H rd, rs MUST set bits 15:0 of rd equal to bits 15:0 of rs and MUST set all bits of rd more significant than bit 15 to zero, producing an XLEN-wide result.
RULE 23: ZEXT.H rd, rs MUST not modify any architectural state other than the destination register rd.

INSTRUCTION: ZIP
FORMAT: zip rd, rs1
RULE 1: ZIP is available only when the Zbk b (Bit-manipulation for Cryptography) extension is implemented.
RULE 2: ZIP must read the value in rs, perform the architectural bit-interleave operation on that value, and write the resulting word to rd.
RULE 3: The ZIP instruction is defined only for implementations where XLEN = 32; on any implementation with a different XLEN the ZIP encoding is reserved.
RULE 4: For each integer i with 0 ≤ i ≤ 15, execution of the ZIP instruction writes the i-th bit of the source register (rs1) into bit position 2·i of the destination register (rd).
RULE 5: For each integer i with 0 ≤ i ≤ 15, execution of the ZIP instruction writes the (i+16)-th bit of the source register (rs1) into bit position 2·i+1 of the destination register (rd).
RULE 6: The ZIP instruction interleaves the lower half (bits 0–15) of the source register into the even bit positions of the destination register and the upper half (bits 16–31) into the odd bit positions of the destination register.
RULE 7: The result produced by the ZIP instruction is the bitwise inverse of the UNZIP instruction, such that applying UNZIP to the destination register yields the original source register value.
RULE 8: ZIP performs a bit-interleave operation, producing a destination value in which the bits of the two source operands are interleaved.
RULE 9: ZIP rd, rs1 reads the 32-bit integer value from source register rs1, applies a bit-interleave (or de-interleave) transformation to that value, and writes the resulting 32-bit integer to destination register rd.

REGISTER: cycle
NUMBER: 0xc00
MODE: U-mode
WIDTH: 64
FIELDS: 63..0=COUNT
EXTENSIONS: -
RULE 1: Implicit reads of the cycle CSR are ordered as device input.
RULE 2: A read of the cycle CSR is classified as device input for the purposes of the FENCE instruction.
RULE 3: A write to the cycle CSR is classified as device output for the purposes of the FENCE instruction.
RULE 4: Accesses to the cycle CSR are weakly ordered by default under the RVWMO memory consistency model.
RULE 5: For base ISAs with XLEN ≥ 64, the RDCYCLE pseudoinstruction reads the full 64-bit value of the cycle CSR.
RULE 6: The cycle counter can be read using the canonical csrrs rd, cycle, x0 instruction as well as the read-only CSRRC, CSRRSI, and CSRRCI forms.
RULE 7: The RDCYCLE pseudoinstruction reads the low XLEN bits of the cycle CSR.
RULE 8: If the entire core is paused (clock-gated or powered-down), the cycle count should not increase.
RULE 9: On some simple platforms, the cycle counter might serve as the real-time clock, causing RDTIME and RDCYCLE to return identical values.
RULE 10: The presented code sequence ensures that a consistent 64-bit cycle counter value is read even if the lower half overflows between the reads.
RULE 11: The cycle CSR is located at address 0xC00 and is designated as unprivileged read-only (URO).
RULE 12: The cycleh CSR is located at address 0xC80 and is designated as unprivileged read-only (URO).
RULE 13: The cycle CSR provides a cycle counter that is accessed by the RDCYCLE instruction.
RULE 14: When the RDCYCLE instruction reads CSR 0xC00, the value returned equals the current cycle counter.
RULE 15: The mcycle register is located at address 0xB00 and provides the Machine cycle counter.
RULE 16: The mcyclecfg register is located at address 0x321 and provides the Machine cycle counter configuration register.
RULE 17: In S-mode, when the indirect CSR mapping entry has siselect equal to 0x40, the first mapped register (sireg) is the cycle register.
RULE 18: In S-mode, when the indirect CSR mapping entry has siselect equal to 0x40, the second mapped register (sireg2) is the cyclecfg register.
RULE 19: In S-mode, when the indirect CSR mapping entry has siselect equal to 0x40, the third mapped register (sireg3) selects none and therefore does not select a cycle-related register.
RULE 20: In S-mode, when the indirect CSR mapping entry has siselect equal to 0x40, the fourth mapped register (sireg4) is the cycleh register.
RULE 21: In S-mode, when the indirect CSR mapping entry has siselect equal to 0x40, the fifth mapped register (sireg5) is the cyclecfgh register.
RULE 22: In S-mode, when the indirect CSR mapping entry has siselect equal to 0x40, the sixth mapped register (sireg6) selects none and therefore does not select a cycle-related register.
RULE 23: The mcycle CSR counts the number of clock cycles executed by the processor core on which the hart is running.
RULE 24: After a hart reset, the mcycle register contains an arbitrary value.
RULE 25: A write to the mcycle CSR stores the specified value into the register.
RULE 26: A write to the mcycle CSR takes effect after the writing instruction has otherwise completed.
RULE 27: If the mcycle CSR is shared between harts on the same core, writes to the mcycle CSR are visible to all those harts.
RULE 28: The cycle counter continues to increment regardless of any reads or writes to the mcounteren register.
RULE 29: When the CY bit in mcounteren is clear, attempts to read the cycle CSR while executing in S-mode or U-mode cause an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 30: When the CY bit in mcounteren is set, access to the cycle CSR is permitted in the next implemented privilege mode (S-mode if implemented, otherwise U-mode).
RULE 31: The cycle CSR is a read-only shadow of the mcycle register.
RULE 32: In harts that support U-mode, the CY field of the mcounteren register, which controls access to the cycle CSR, must be implemented, is WARL, and may be read-only zero.
RULE 33: In harts that support U-mode, when the CY field of mcounteren is read-only zero, reads of the cycle CSR from a less-privileged mode cause an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 34: When the CY bit in the mcountinhibit register is clear, the mcycle CSR increments on each cycle.
RULE 35: When the CY bit in the mcountinhibit register is set, the mcycle CSR does not increment on any cycle.
RULE 36: If the mcountinhibit register is not implemented, the implementation behaves as if the CY bit were clear, causing the mcycle CSR to increment on each cycle.
RULE 37: When the mcycle CSR is shared between harts on the same core, the mcountinhibit.CY field is also shared, and writes to mcountinhibit.CY are visible to those harts, thereby controlling whether the shared mcycle CSR increments on each cycle.
RULE 38: By default the cycle counter is not filtered by privilege mode.
RULE 39: The privilege-mode filtering applied to the cycle counter is the same as that applied to the instret counter.
RULE 40: Bit 62 of mcyclecfg, named MINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in machine mode.
RULE 41: Bit 61 of mcyclecfg, named SINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in supervisor or hypervisor mode.
RULE 42: Bit 60 of mcyclecfg, named UINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in user mode.
RULE 43: Bit 59 of mcyclecfg, named VSINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in virtual-supervisor mode.
RULE 44: Bit 58 of mcyclecfg, named VUINH, when set inhibits counting of cycle events while the processor is executing in virtual-user mode.
RULE 45: If all INH bits (MINH, SINH, UINH, VSINH, VUINH) in mcyclecfg are zero, counting of cycle events is enabled in all privilege modes.
RULE 46: For any INH bit in positions 61 through 58 of mcyclecfg, if the associated privilege mode is not implemented, that bit is read-only zero.
RULE 47: The cycle counter will increment for each CPU cycle while the CPU is executing in a non-inhibited privilege mode.
RULE 48: When mcounteren[0] = 1 and menvcfg.CDE = 1, the cycle register may be read or written via the indirect CSRs while siselect = 0x40.
RULE 49: When siselect = 0x40, accesses to sireg select the low 32 bits of the cycle counter (cycle).
RULE 50: When siselect = 0x40, accesses to sireg4 select the high half of the cycle counter (cycleh).
RULE 51: When siselect = 0x40, accesses to sireg2 select the cycle configuration register (cyclecfg).
RULE 52: When siselect = 0x40, accesses to sireg5 select the high half of the cycle configuration register (cyclecfgh).
RULE 53: If menvcfg.CDE = 0, any access to the cycle register via sireg* raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 54: If XLEN = 64, any access to the cycleh register via sireg4 raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 55: If XLEN = 64, any access to the cyclecfgh register via sireg5 raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 56: If mcounteren[0] = 0, any access to the cycle register, cycleh, cyclecfg, or cyclecfgh via the indirect CSRs raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 57: If the Smcntrpmf extension is implemented, bit 62 of the cyclecfg register accessed via sireg* is read-only, reads as 0, and writes to that bit have no effect.
RULE 58: If the Smcntrpmf extension is implemented, bit 62 of the cyclecfgh register accessed via sireg* is read-only, reads as 0, and writes to that bit have no effect.
RULE 59: If any required extension for the cycle register state is not implemented, attempts from M-mode or S-mode to access the cycle register via the indirect CSRs raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 60: If any required extension for the cycleh register state is not implemented, attempts from M-mode or S-mode to access the cycleh register via the indirect CSRs raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 61: In VU-mode, any access to the cycle register via sireg* raises a virtual-instruction exception.
RULE 62: When vsiselect = 0x40, any access to the cycle register via vsireg* from M-mode or S-mode raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 63: In VS-mode, an access to the cycle register via sireg* raises an illegal-instruction exception when menvcfg.CDE = 0.
RULE 64: In VS-mode, an access to the cycle register via sireg* raises a virtual-instruction exception when menvcfg.CDE = 1.
RULE 65: The SCTRCLR instruction must set the cycle counter field of the CTR register to zero and must also set the CCV field to zero.
RULE 66: Any read of the cycle-related registers ctrsource, ctrtarget, or ctrdata that occurs after execution of SCTRCLR and before the next qualified control transfer must return zero.
RULE 67: The first recorded control transfer after execution of SCTRCLR must have its CCV field in the cycle data (ctrdata.CCV) equal to zero.
RULE 68: The elapsed cycle counter (CtrCycleCounter) increments at the same rate as the mcycle counter.
RULE 69: Only cycles while CTR is active are counted, where active implies that the current privilege mode is enabled for recording and CTR is not frozen.
RULE 70: The cycle count exponent CCE holds 0 if the CtrCycleCounter value is less than 4096; otherwise CCE holds the index of the most significant one bit in the CtrCycleCounter value minus 11.
RULE 71: The cycle count mantissa CCM holds the CtrCycleCounter bits CCE+10 down to CCE-1.
RULE 72: The CtrCycleCounter is reset on writes to x ctrctl and on execution of SCTRCLR to ensure that any accumulated cycle counts do not persist across a context switch.
RULE 73: Unimplemented CCE bits, which are part of the cycle count exponent, are read-only 0.
RULE 74: When CCE>1, the granularity of the reported cycle count is reduced.
RULE 75: When CCE=3, the bottom 2 bits of the cycle counter are not reported, and thus the reported value increments only every 4 cycles.
RULE 76: The cycle count (CC) value saturates when all implemented bits in CCM and CCE are 1.
RULE 77: The next record will have CCV=0 after a write to x ctrctl or execution of SCTRCLR, since the cycle counter is reset.
RULE 78: The implementation should provide a mechanism to modify counter values, and this mechanism must also apply to the cycle counter.
RULE 79: If the CY bit in scounteren is clear, a read of the cycle register while executing in U-mode causes an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 80: If the CY bit in scounteren is set, access to the cycle register from U-mode is permitted.
RULE 81: If the CY bit in scounteren is read-only zero, a U-mode read of the cycle register causes an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 82: The writability of the CY bit in scounteren is not affected by the setting of the CY bit in mcounteren.
RULE 83: A U-mode read of the cycle register causes an illegal-instruction exception unless both the CY bit in scounteren and the CY bit in mcounteren are set.
RULE 84: If both the CY bit in scounteren and the CY bit in mcounteren are set, a U-mode read of the cycle register is permitted.
RULE 85: When the CY bit in the hcounteren register is clear, attempts to read the cycle register while V=1 will cause a virtual-instruction exception if the CY bit in mcounteren is 1.
RULE 86: When the CY bit in the hcounteren register is set, access to the cycle register is permitted while V=1 unless prevented for some other reason.
RULE 87: In VU-mode, the cycle register is readable only if the CY bit is set in both hcounteren and scounteren.
RULE 88: The CY bit in hcounteren may be implemented as read-only zero, which causes reads of the cycle register to cause an exception when V=1.
RULE 89: When the 64-bit cycle counter wraps, the mcause or scause register is set to exception code 13 (counter-overflow interrupt).
RULE 90: When V=1 and an attempt to access a cycle counter CSR is HS-qualified but is prevented by insufficient privilege or by a supervisor or hypervisor CSR such as scounteren or hcounteren, a virtual-instruction exception with code 22 is taken.
RULE 91: When XLEN>32, any attempt to access a high-half cycle CSR (e.g., cycleh) raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 92: In VS-mode, accessing a non-high-half cycle CSR (cycle) while the corresponding hcounteren bit is 0 and the corresponding mcounteren bit is 1 raises a virtual-instruction exception with code 22.
RULE 93: In VU-mode, accessing a non-high-half cycle CSR (cycle) while the corresponding bit in either hcounteren or scounteren is 0 and the corresponding mcounteren bit is 1 raises a virtual-instruction exception with code 22.
RULE 94: When a virtual-instruction exception is taken due to any of the above cycle-counter conditions, the mtval or stval register is written in the same manner as for an illegal-instruction exception.

REGISTER: fcsr
NUMBER: 0x003
MODE: U-mode
WIDTH: 32
FIELDS: 7..5=FRM, 4..4=NV, 3..3=DZ, 2..2=OF, 1..1=UF, 0..0=NX
EXTENSIONS: D, F, Q, Zdinx, Zfinx, Zhinx
RULE 1: The fcsr register is not visible to other harts.
RULE 2: Bits 4, 3, 2, 1, and 0 of the fcsr register are aliases of the corresponding bits in the fflags CSR and are tracked as independent units.
RULE 3: The whole fcsr register is an alias of the frm CSR and is tracked as a single independent unit.
RULE 4: Bits 7, 6, and 5 of the fcsr register are aliases of the frm CSR and are tracked as independent units.
RULE 5: Bits 31-8 of fcsr are reserved for other standard extensions, and if those extensions are not present implementations shall ignore writes to these bits and shall return zero for these bits when fcsr is read.
RULE 6: The FSCSR instruction swaps the value in fcsr by copying the original fcsr value into integer register rd and then writing a new value taken from integer register rs1 into fcsr.
RULE 7: The FRRM instruction reads the rounding-mode field frm (bits 7-5 of fcsr) and copies it into the least-significant three bits of integer register rd, setting all other bits of rd to zero.
RULE 8: The FSRM instruction swaps the rounding-mode field frm by copying the original bits 7-5 of fcsr into integer register rd and then writing the three least-significant bits of integer register rs1 into bits 7-5 of fcsr.
RULE 9: The FRFLAGS instruction reads the accrued-exception-flags field fflags (bits 4-0 of fcsr) and copies it into integer register rd, zero-extending the value to the full width of rd.
RULE 10: The FSFLAGS instruction swaps the accrued-exception-flags field by copying the original bits 4-0 of fcsr into integer register rd and then writing the five least-significant bits of integer register rs1 into bits 4-0 of fcsr.
RULE 11: Floating-point operations use either a static rounding mode encoded in the instruction or the dynamic rounding mode held in frm, and an instruction encoding of rm=111 selects the dynamic rounding mode held in frm.
RULE 12: The behavior of floating-point instructions that depend on rounding mode is reserved when executed with a reserved static rounding mode (encodings 101-110) or a reserved dynamic rounding mode (encodings 101-111).
RULE 13: Implementations may raise an illegal-instruction exception when a floating-point instruction is executed with a reserved dynamic rounding mode, and such behavior remains valid under the weakened specification.
RULE 14: The accrued exception flags in fcsr indicate which exception conditions have arisen on any floating-point arithmetic instruction since the flags were last reset by software.
RULE 15: The base RISC-V ISA does not provide a mechanism to generate a trap on the setting of any floating-point exception flag in fcsr.
RULE 16: Bits 7-5 of fcsr encode the rounding mode with the following meanings: 000 = round to nearest, ties to even (RNE); 001 = round towards zero (RTZ); 010 = round down towards –∞ (RDN); 011 = round up towards +∞ (RUP); 100 = round to nearest, ties to max magnitude (RMM); 101 and 110 are reserved for future use; 111 is reserved in the register and is used in an instruction's rm field to select the dynamic rounding mode.
RULE 17: Bits 4-0 of fcsr encode the accrued exception flags with the following bit assignments: bit 4 = Invalid Operation (NV); bit 3 = Divide by Zero (DZ); bit 2 = Overflow (OF); bit 1 = Underflow (UF); bit 0 = Inexact (NX).
RULE 18: When the Zfinx extension is implemented, the mstatus.FS field is hard-wired to 0, and this hard-wiring removes any effect of the FS field on the trapping behavior of fcsr accesses.
RULE 19: When the mstatus.FS field is hard-wired to 0, the FS field no longer affects the trapping behavior of floating-point instructions or fcsr accesses.
RULE 20: The fcsr has URW privilege, meaning it is readable and writable in unprivileged mode.
RULE 21: The fflags component of the fcsr is URW (unprivileged read/write).
RULE 22: The frm component of the fcsr is URW (unprivileged read/write).
RULE 23: When an instruction explicitly or implicitly writes the fcsr without altering its contents while FS is Initial or Clean, it is implementation-defined whether FS transitions to Dirty.
RULE 24: Changing the FS field has no effect on the contents of the fcsr.
RULE 25: Setting FS=Off does not destroy the contents of the fcsr.
RULE 26: Setting FS=Initial does not clear the contents of the fcsr.
RULE 27: The FCSR bit of a state-enable CSR determines whether accesses to the fcsr register are permitted when floating-point instructions operate on integer (x) registers under the Zfinx, Zdinx, and related extensions.
RULE 28: When misa.F=1, the FCSR bit of mstateen0, hstateen0, and sstateen0 is read-only zero, pertaining to the fcsr register.
RULE 29: When state-enable CSRs are implemented, misa.F=0, and the FCSR bit of a controlling stateen0 CSR is zero, every floating-point instruction raises an illegal-instruction exception or, if applicable, a virtual-instruction exception as if it accessed the fcsr register, regardless of the actual access.

REGISTER: fflags
NUMBER: 0x001
MODE: U-mode
WIDTH: 32
FIELDS: 4..4=NV, 3..3=DZ, 2..2=OF, 1..1=UF, 0..0=NX
EXTENSIONS: D, F, Q, V
RULE 1: An access to the fcsr CSR also affects the fflags CSR.
RULE 2: The Accrued Exception Flags field named fflags occupies bits 4-0 of the floating-point control and status register (fcsr).
RULE 3: The FRFLAGS instruction reads the current value of fflags and copies it into integer register rd, placing the flag bits in rd bits 4-0 and clearing all other bits of rd to zero.
RULE 4: The FSFLAGS instruction returns the original value of fflags in integer register rd.
RULE 5: The FSFLAGS instruction writes a new value to fflags using the three least-significant bits of integer register rs1 as the source value.
RULE 6: The FSFLAGS instruction updates fflags with the low five bits of rs1, replacing the previous flag contents.
RULE 7: Whenever a floating-point arithmetic instruction encounters an exception condition, the corresponding bit(s) in fflags become set.
RULE 8: Once set, the bits in fflags remain set until software resets the field.
RULE 9: Each of the five bits in fflags (bits 4-0) corresponds to one of the exception mnemonics NV, DZ, OF, UF, and NX, representing Invalid Operation, Divide by Zero, Overflow, Underflow, and Inexact respectively.
RULE 10: Setting a flag bit in fflags never generates a trap in the base RISC-V ISA.
RULE 11: A vector floating-point exception occurring at any active floating-point element sets the standard FP exception flags in the fflags register.
RULE 12: An inactive floating-point element does not set the FP exception flags in the fflags register.
RULE 13: The fflags CSR is accessible with unprivileged read/write (URW) privilege.
RULE 14: The fcsr CSR, which incorporates the fflags field, is accessible with unprivileged read/write (URW) privilege.
RULE 15: Changing the setting of the FS field has no effect on the contents of the fflags CSR.
RULE 16: Setting FS=Off does not destroy the contents of the fflags CSR.
RULE 17: Setting FS=Initial does not clear the contents of the fflags CSR.

REGISTER: frm
NUMBER: 0x002
MODE: U-mode
WIDTH: 32
FIELDS: 2..0=ROUNDINGMODE
EXTENSIONS: F, V, Zvfbfmin, Zvfbfwma
RULE 1: The frm register is listed as an alias of the fcsr CSR.
RULE 2: The fcsr CSR lists frm as one of its aliases.
RULE 3: Bits 7-5 of the fcsr CSR are an alias of the frm register.
RULE 4: Modifying bits 7-5 of the fcsr CSR changes the value of the frm register.
RULE 5: The FRRM instruction reads the frm field and copies its value into the least-significant three bits of integer register rd while zeroing all other bits of rd.
RULE 6: The FSRM instruction first copies the original frm value into integer register rd and then writes a new value taken from the three least-significant bits of integer register rs1 into the frm field.
RULE 7: When the rm field of a floating-point instruction is binary 111, the instruction selects the dynamic rounding mode held in frm.
RULE 8: When frm holds the binary value 000, it specifies the rounding mode RNE – Round to Nearest, ties to Even.
RULE 9: When frm holds the binary value 001, it specifies the rounding mode RTZ – Round towards Zero.
RULE 10: When frm holds the binary value 010, it specifies the rounding mode RDN – Round Down (towards –∞).
RULE 11: When frm holds the binary value 011, it specifies the rounding mode RUP – Round Up (towards +∞).
RULE 12: When frm holds the binary value 100, it specifies the rounding mode RMM – Round to Nearest, ties to Max Magnitude.
RULE 13: When frm holds the binary value 101, it is a reserved value for future use.
RULE 14: When frm holds the binary value 110, it is a reserved value for future use.
RULE 15: When frm holds the binary value 111, it is a reserved value and is used for dynamic rounding-mode selection in the rm field.
RULE 16: The binary values 101, 110, and 111 of frm are reserved rounding modes.
RULE 17: If a floating-point instruction that depends on rounding mode is executed with a reserved rounding mode, including any of the reserved frm values, the behavior of the instruction is reserved.
RULE 18: When the rm field of a scalar floating-point instruction is encoded as DYN (binary 111), the instruction uses the rounding mode specified in the frm CSR.
RULE 19: The sum is rounded according to the frm register.
RULE 20: All vector floating-point operations use the dynamic rounding mode specified in the frm register.
RULE 21: If the frm field contains an invalid rounding mode, any vector floating-point instruction, including those that do not depend on the rounding mode, causes the operation to be reserved.
RULE 22: If the vector length register (vl) equals zero, any use of the frm field by a vector floating-point instruction is reserved.
RULE 23: If the vector start register (vstart) is greater than or equal to vl, any use of the frm field by a vector floating-point instruction is reserved.
RULE 24: The vector floating-point/integer conversion instructions vfcvt.xu.f.v, vfcvt.x.f.v, vfcvt.rtz.xu.f.v, vfcvt.rtz.x.f.v, vfcvt.f.xu.v, and vfcvt.f.x.v use the dynamic rounding mode specified in the frm register.
RULE 25: The rtz variants vfcvt.rtz.xu.f.v and vfcvt.rtz.x.f.v do not use the rounding mode in the frm register and instead round towards zero.
RULE 26: The frm register has privilege level URW (User-Read/Write).

REGISTER: hcounteren
NUMBER: 0x606
MODE: HS-mode
WIDTH: 32
FIELDS: 31..31=HPM31, 30..30=HPM30, 29..29=HPM29, 28..28=HPM28, 27..27=HPM27, 26..26=HPM26, 25..25=HPM25, 24..24=HPM24, 23..23=HPM23, 22..22=HPM22, 21..21=HPM21, 20..20=HPM20, 19..19=HPM19, 18..18=HPM18, 17..17=HPM17, 16..16=HPM16, 15..15=HPM15, 14..14=HPM14, 13..13=HPM13, 12..12=HPM12, 11..11=HPM11, 10..10=HPM10, 9..9=HPM9, 8..8=HPM8, 7..7=HPM7, 6..6=HPM6, 5..5=HPM5, 4..4=HPM4, 3..3=HPM3, 2..2=IR, 1..1=TM, 0..0=CY
EXTENSIONS: H
RULE 1: The hcounteren CSR is readable and writable in hypervisor privilege mode (HRW).
RULE 2: Access to the vstimecmp register via stimecmp in VS-mode is permitted only if the TM bit in hcounteren does not prevent such access and the register is implemented.
RULE 3: In VS-mode, a scountovf bit X is readable only if the corresponding hcounteren bit X is set.
RULE 4: If the hcounteren bit X is clear in VS-mode, reads of scountovf bit X return zero.
RULE 5: hcounteren is a CSR that is provided to HS-mode.
RULE 6: hcounteren is not provided to VS-mode.
RULE 7: If a CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit in hcounteren is clear, a read of the corresponding cycle, time, instret, or hpmcounter n register while V=1 causes a virtual-instruction exception provided the same bit in mcounteren is 1.
RULE 8: If a CY, TM, IR, or HPM n bit in hcounteren is set, access to the corresponding register is permitted while V=1 unless some other condition prevents it.
RULE 9: In VU-mode, a counter register is readable only if the applicable bits are set in both hcounteren and scounteren.
RULE 10: If the TM bit in hcounteren is clear, an access to the vstimecmp register (via stimecmp) while executing in VS-mode causes a virtual-instruction exception when the TM bit in mcounteren is set.
RULE 11: If the TM bit in hcounteren and the TM bit in mcounteren are both set, access to the vstimecmp register (if implemented) is permitted in VS-mode.
RULE 12: Any bit in hcounteren may be read-only zero, and reads of the associated counter cause a virtual-instruction exception when V=1.
RULE 13: All bits in hcounteren are WARL fields.
RULE 14: When V=1, if an HS-qualified instruction is prevented from executing because it is expressly disabled by the hypervisor CSR hcounteren, a virtual-instruction exception with cause 22 is raised instead of an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 15: In VS-mode, if a non-high-half counter CSR is accessed and the corresponding bit in hcounteren is 0 while the corresponding bit in mcounteren is 1, a virtual-instruction exception is raised.
RULE 16: In VU-mode, if a non-high-half counter CSR is accessed and the corresponding bit in either hcounteren or scounteren is 0 while the corresponding bit in mcounteren is 1, a virtual-instruction exception is raised.

REGISTER: hedeleg
NUMBER: 0x602
MODE: HS-mode

FIELDS: 23..23=SGPF, 22..22=VI, 21..21=LGPF, 20..20=IGPF, 15..15=SPF, 13..13=LPF, 12..12=IPF, 11..11=EM, 10..10=EVS, 9..9=ES, 8..8=EU, 7..7=SAF, 6..6=SAM, 5..5=LAF, 4..4=LAM, 3..3=B, 2..2=II, 1..1=IAF, 0..0=IAM
EXTENSIONS: -
RULE 1: hedeleg is listed with access type HRW, indicating hypervisor-read/write permission.
RULE 2: The P1P13 bit in the mstateen0 register controls access to the hedeleg register introduced by Privileged Specification Version 1.13.
RULE 3: The hedeleg CSR is provided to HS-mode.
RULE 4: The hedeleg CSR is not provided to VS-mode.
RULE 5: hedeleg is a 64-bit read/write register.
RULE 6: A synchronous trap that has been delegated to HS-mode using medeleg is further delegated to VS-mode if V = 1 before the trap and the corresponding hedeleg bit is set.
RULE 7: Each bit of hedeleg shall be either writable or read-only 0.
RULE 8: Bit 0 of hedeleg must be writable if IALIGN = 32.
RULE 9: When XLEN = 64, no alias register for hedeleg exists.
RULE 10: Bit 1 of hedeleg is writable.
RULE 11: Bit 2 of hedeleg is writable.
RULE 12: Bit 3 of hedeleg is writable.

RULE 14: Bit 5 of hedeleg is writable.
RULE 15: Bit 6 of hedeleg is writable.
RULE 16: Bit 7 of hedeleg is writable.
RULE 17: Bit 8 of hedeleg is writable.
RULE 18: Bit 9 of hedeleg is read-only 0.
RULE 19: Bit 10 of hedeleg is read-only 0.
RULE 20: Bit 11 of hedeleg is read-only 0.

RULE 22: Bit 13 of hedeleg is writable.

RULE 25: Bit 18 of hedeleg is writable.
RULE 26: Bit 19 of hedeleg is writable.
