RULE 42: When mstateen0.CTR = 0, qualified control transfers executed in privilege modes less privileged than M-mode implicitly update entry registers and sctrstatus.
RULE 43: If the H extension is implemented and mstateen0.CTR = 1, the hstateen0.CTR bit controls access to supervisor CTR state when V = 1.
RULE 44: When mstateen0.CTR = 0, hstateen0.CTR is read-only 0.
RULE 45: When mstateen0.CTR = 1 and hstateen0.CTR = 0, VS-mode accesses to supervisor CTR state raise a virtual-instruction exception.
RULE 46: When mstateen0.CTR = 1 and hstateen0.CTR = 0, execution of the SCTRCLR instruction in VS-mode raises a virtual-instruction exception.
RULE 47: If the SRMCFG field of mstateen0 is 0, any attempt to access the srmcfg CSR from a privilege mode less privileged than M-mode MUST raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 48: If the SRMCFG field of mstateen0 is 1 or the Smstateen extension is not implemented, any attempt to access the srmcfg CSR while V=1 MUST raise a virtual-instruction exception.

REGISTER: mstateen1
NUMBER: 0x30d
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: 64
FIELDS: 63..63=SE0
EXTENSIONS: Smstateen
RULE 1: mstateen1 is a machine-read/write CSR located at address 0x30D.
RULE 2: The architectural privilege level for accessing mstateen1 is MRW (machine-read/write).
RULE 3: The CSR named mstateen1h, which provides access to the upper 32 bits of mstateen1, resides at address 0x31D and is also machine-read/write.
RULE 4: Each bit of mstateen1 controls less-privileged access to the corresponding extension state for extensions that do not have a full XS field in sstatus.
RULE 5: The mstateen1 CSR controls access to state at all less-privileged privilege levels but does not control access at machine level itself.
RULE 6: When mstateen1 prevents access to state by a less-privileged privilege mode, an instruction in that mode that would read or write the protected state raises an illegal-instruction exception, or, if executing in VS or VU mode under the virtual-instruction exception conditions, raises a virtual-instruction exception instead.
RULE 7: For every bit that has a defined purpose in an sstateen CSR, the same bit is defined in mstateen1 to control access below machine level to the same state.
RULE 8: The upper 32 bits of mstateen1 (bits 63-32) control access to state that is inherently inaccessible to user level, and therefore no corresponding enable bits exist in the supervisor-level sstateen CSR.
RULE 9: Bits in mstateen1 that are defined to control state not implemented by a hart, as well as all reserved bits not yet given a defined meaning, are read-only zeros for that hart.
RULE 10: For every bit in mstateen1 that is zero—whether a read-only zero or a writable zero—the same bit appears as a read-only zero in the matching hstateen1 and sstateen1 CSRs.
RULE 11: On reset, all writable bits of mstateen1 are initialized by hardware to zeros.
RULE 12: Bit 63 of mstateen1 is defined to control access to the matching sstateen1 and hstateen1 CSRs.
RULE 13: Bit 63 of mstateen1 may be a read-only zero only if the hypervisor extension is not implemented and the matching sstateen1 CSR is entirely read-only zeros; in that case, machine-level software should emulate attempts to access the affected sstateen1 from S-mode by ignoring writes and returning zero for reads.
RULE 14: After reset, all writable bits of the mstateen1 CSR are initialized to zero.

REGISTER: mstateen2
NUMBER: 0x30e
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: 64
FIELDS: 63..63=SE0
EXTENSIONS: -
RULE 1: The CSR at address 0x30E is named mstateen2 and has MRW privilege.
RULE 2: The CSR at address 0x31E is named mstateen2h and has MRW privilege.
RULE 3: Each bit of mstateen2 controls less-privileged access to the state of the corresponding extension.
RULE 4: mstateen2 controls access to extension state for privilege modes below machine mode, but does not affect access for machine mode itself.
RULE 5: If a bit in mstateen2 is zero, an attempt in a less-privileged mode to execute an instruction that reads or writes the protected state raises an illegal-instruction exception, or raises a virtual-instruction exception instead when executing in VS or VU mode and the virtual-instruction exception conditions apply.
RULE 6: Each standard-defined writable bit of mstateen2 is WARL and may be either read-only zero or read-only one, subject to the specified conditions.
RULE 7: For any bit of mstateen2 that is defined to control state not implemented by a hart, that bit is a read-only zero for that hart.
RULE 8: All reserved bits of mstateen2 are read-only zeros.
RULE 9: For each bit of mstateen2 that is zero, the corresponding bit in hstateen2 and sstateen2 is a read-only zero.
RULE 10: A bit in sstateen2 cannot be read-only one unless the corresponding bit in mstateen2 is read-only one (and, if present, the corresponding bit in hstateen2 is also read-only one).
RULE 11: A bit in hstateen2 cannot be read-only one unless the corresponding bit in mstateen2 is read-only one.
RULE 12: After reset, all writable bits of mstateen2 are hardware-initialized to zero.
RULE 13: Bit 63 of mstateen2 controls access to sstateen2 and hstateen2.
RULE 14: Bit 63 of mstateen2 may be read-only zero only if the hypervisor extension is not implemented and sstateen2 is entirely read-only zeros.
RULE 15: After reset, all writable bits of the machine-level CSR mstateen2 are initialized to zero.
RULE 16: Machine-level software may write 1s to writable bits of mstateen2 to enable less-privileged access to the corresponding state.
RULE 17: When a writable bit of mstateen2 is written with a 1, the matching bit in the corresponding hstateen CSR, if that hstateen CSR exists, must be written with 0.
RULE 18: When a writable bit of mstateen2 is written with a 1 and the same-position bit exists in an sstateen CSR, the matching bit in that sstateen CSR must be written with 0.
RULE 19: When bit 63 of mstateen2 is written with a 1, all bits of the corresponding hstateen CSR must be written with 0.

REGISTER: mstateen3
NUMBER: 0x30f
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: 64
FIELDS: 63..63=SE0
EXTENSIONS: H, Smstateen, Ssstateen
RULE 1: The privilege encoding for mstateen3 is MRW, indicating that the register is machine-read/write accessible.
RULE 2: Every bit in mstateen3 controls whether software in less-privileged modes (S-mode, U-mode, VS-mode, VU-mode) may read or write the corresponding piece of extension state.
RULE 3: mstateen3 does not restrict machine-mode accesses and only restricts accesses from lower-privilege modes.
RULE 4: If mstateen3 prevents access to state for a privilege mode, an attempt in that mode to execute an instruction that would read or write the protected state raises an illegal-instruction exception, or raises a virtual-instruction exception instead when executing in VS- or VU-mode under the circumstances that cause a virtual-instruction exception.
RULE 5: Bit 63 of mstateen3 controls access to the matching sstateen3 and hstateen3 CSRs.
RULE 6: Bit 63 of mstateen3 may be read-only zero only if the hypervisor extension is not implemented and sstateen3 is all read-only zeros.
RULE 7: After reset, every writable bit in mstateen3 is hardware-initialized to zero.
RULE 8: Each standard-defined bit of mstateen3 is WARL and may be either read-only zero or read-only one.
RULE 9: Any bit of mstateen3 that is defined to control state that the hart does not implement is read-only zero.
RULE 10: All reserved bits of mstateen3 that have not been given a defined meaning are read-only zero.
RULE 11: Any bit that is zero in mstateen3, whether read-only zero or writable zero, appears as a read-only zero in the matching sstateen3 and hstateen3 CSRs.
RULE 12: A read-only-one bit in sstateen3 requires the corresponding bit in mstateen3 to be read-only one.
RULE 13: A read-only-one bit in hstateen3 requires the corresponding bit in mstateen3 to be read-only one.
RULE 14: After reset, all writable bits of mstateen3 are initialized to zero.

REGISTER: mstatus
NUMBER: 0x300
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..63=SD, 42..42=MDT, 41..41=MPELP, 39..39=MPV, 38..38=GVA, 37..37=MBE, 36..36=SBE, 35..34=SXL, 33..32=UXL, 23..23=SPELP, 22..22=TSR, 21..21=TW, 20..20=TVM, 19..19=MXR, 18..18=SUM, 17..17=MPRV, 16..15=XS, 14..13=FS, 12..11=MPP, 10..9=VS, 8..8=SPP, 7..7=MPIE, 6..6=UBE, 5..5=SPIE, 3..3=MIE, 1..1=SIE
EXTENSIONS: -
RULE 1: If the TW bit in mstatus is set, the privilege mode is not M mode, and a WRS.NTO instruction does not complete within an implementation-specific bounded time limit, then the WRS.NTO instruction MUST cause an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 2: In VS or VU mode, when the VTW bit in hstatus is set, the TW bit in mstatus is clear, and a WRS.NTO instruction does not complete within an implementation-specific bounded time limit, then the WRS.NTO instruction MUST cause a virtual-instruction exception.
RULE 3: Whether a CMO instruction is permitted to access a cache block may depend on the state of the MPRV bit in mstatus.
RULE 4: Whether a CMO instruction is permitted to access a cache block may depend on the state of the MPV bit in mstatus.
RULE 5: Whether a CMO instruction is permitted to access a cache block may depend on the state of the MPP field in mstatus.
RULE 6: Whether a CMO instruction is permitted to access a cache block may depend on the state of the SUM bit in mstatus.
RULE 7: Whether a CMO instruction is permitted to access a cache block may depend on the state of the MXR bit in mstatus.
RULE 8: When the Zfinx extension is implemented, the FS field in the mstatus register is hardwired to 0.
RULE 9: When the Zfinx extension is implemented, the FS field in the mstatus register does not affect the trapping behavior of floating-point instructions or accesses to the fcsr register.
RULE 10: If mstatus.VS equals Off and an attempt is made to execute any vector instruction or to access any vector CSR, an illegal-instruction exception is raised.
RULE 11: If mstatus.VS equals Initial or Clean and an instruction that changes vector state is executed (including accesses to vector CSRs), then mstatus.VS is changed to Dirty.
RULE 12: When mstatus.VS equals Initial or Clean, an implementation may change mstatus.VS to Dirty at any time, even when there is no change in vector state.
RULE 13: If mstatus.VS equals Dirty, then mstatus.SD is set to 1.
RULE 14: When V=1 and either vsstatus.VS or mstatus.VS is Off, attempts to execute any vector instruction or to access any vector CSR raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 15: When V=1 and neither vsstatus.VS nor mstatus.VS is Off, execution of any instruction that changes vector state, including accesses to vector CSRs, changes both mstatus.VS and vsstatus.VS to Dirty.
RULE 16: If mstatus.VS is Dirty, then mstatus.SD is 1.
RULE 17: If mstatus.VS is not Dirty, then mstatus.SD is set in accordance with existing specifications.
RULE 18: If the mstatus.FS field is Off then any attempt to execute a vector floating-point instruction will raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 19: Any vector floating-point instruction that modifies any floating-point extension state must set the mstatus.FS field to Dirty.
RULE 20: When the hypervisor extension is implemented and V=1, if the mstatus.FS field is Off then any attempt to execute a vector floating-point instruction will raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 21: When the hypervisor extension is implemented and V=1, if either the vsstatus.FS field or the mstatus.FS field is Off then any attempt to execute a vector floating-point instruction will raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 22: When the hypervisor extension is implemented and V=1, any vector floating-point instruction that modifies any floating-point extension state must set both mstatus.FS and vsstatus.FS to Dirty.
RULE 23: The mstatus CSR is defined to be accessed at Machine privilege level.
RULE 24: The mstatus CSR has machine-read/write (MRW) access permissions.
RULE 25: The mstatush CSR is defined to be accessed at Machine privilege level.
RULE 26: The mstatush CSR has machine-read/write (MRW) access permissions.
RULE 27: The mstatus register is an MXLEN-bit read/write register that keeps track of and controls the hart's current operating state.
RULE 28: In the mstatush register, bits 30:4 generally contain the same fields that are found in bits 62:36 of the RV64 mstatus register.
RULE 29: The fields SD, SXL, and UXL are not present in the mstatush register.
RULE 30: The global interrupt-enable bits MIE and SIE reside in the low-order bits of mstatus, permitting atomic set or clear with a single CSR instruction.
RULE 31: In mstatus, interrupt enable for any lower-privilege mode w (w < x) is always globally disabled irrespective of the value of the wIE bit.
RULE 32: In mstatus, interrupt enable for any higher-privilege mode y (y > x) is always globally enabled irrespective of the value of the yIE bit.
RULE 33: If supervisor mode is not implemented, the SIE and SPIE fields of mstatus are read-only 0.
RULE 34: The xPP fields in mstatus can hold only privilege modes up to x, resulting in MPP being two bits wide and SPP being one bit wide.
RULE 35: When a trap is taken from privilege mode y into privilege mode x, the mstatus field xPIE is set to the current value of xIE, the mstatus field xIE is cleared to 0, and the mstatus field xPP is written with y.
RULE 36: Executing an xRET instruction (MRET or SRET) sets the mstatus field xIE to the value of xPIE, changes the current privilege mode to the value stored in xPP, sets xPIE in mstatus to 1, writes xPP in mstatus with the least-privileged supported mode (U if U-mode is implemented, otherwise M), and, if the saved privilege mode y is not M, also clears the MPRV bit in mstatus.
RULE 37: The xPP fields in mstatus are WARL fields that may contain only privilege mode x or any implemented privilege mode lower than x, and if privilege mode x is not implemented, the xPP field must be read-only 0.
RULE 38: M-mode software can determine whether a privilege mode is implemented by writing that mode to the MPP field of mstatus and then reading it back.
RULE 39: When a machine implements only U and M privilege modes, a single hardware storage bit in the mstatus MPP field suffices to represent either the binary pattern 00 or 11.
RULE 40: Upon reset, the MDT field in mstatus is set to 1.
RULE 41: When the MDT bit in mstatus is set to 1 by an explicit CSR write, the MIE bit in mstatus is cleared to 0.
RULE 42: On RV64, the clearing of the MIE bit in mstatus to 0 occurs regardless of the value written, if any, to the MIE bit by the same CSR write that sets the MDT bit to 1.
RULE 43: The MIE bit in mstatus may be set to 1 by an explicit CSR write only if the MDT bit in mstatus is already 0, or, on RV64, if the MDT bit is being set to 0 by the same write.
RULE 44: When a trap is taken into M-mode and the MDT bit in mstatus is currently 0, the MDT bit is set to 1 and the trap is delivered as expected.
RULE 45: A trap caused by an RNMI does not set the MDT bit in mstatus.
RULE 46: When executed in M-mode, the MRET instruction sets the MDT bit in mstatus to 0.
RULE 47: When executed in M-mode, the SRET instruction sets the MDT bit in mstatus to 0.
RULE 48: When the MNRET instruction is executed, it sets the MDT bit in mstatus to 0 if the new privilege mode is not M.
RULE 49: If the new privilege mode after executing MRET or SRET is U, VS, or VU, then sstatus.SDT is also set to 0.
RULE 50: If the new privilege mode after executing MRET or SRET is VU, then vsstatus.SDT is also set to 0.
RULE 51: When MNRET sets the MDT bit in mstatus to 0, if the new privilege mode is U, VS, or VU then sstatus.SDT is set to 0.
RULE 52: When MNRET sets the MDT bit in mstatus to 0, if the new privilege mode is VU then vsstatus.SDT is set to 0.
RULE 53: In the mstatus register, the SXL and UXL fields are WARL fields that control the XLEN for S-mode and U-mode, respectively, on RV64 harts.
RULE 54: In the mstatus register, the encoding of the SXL and UXL fields is identical to the encoding of the MXL field in the misa register.
RULE 55: If MXLEN is 64 and S-mode is not supported, the SXL field in the mstatus register is read-only zero.
RULE 56: If MXLEN is 64 and S-mode is supported, the SXL field in the mstatus register is a WARL field that encodes the current SXLEN value.
RULE 57: If MXLEN is 64 and U-mode is not supported, the UXL field in the mstatus register is read-only zero.
RULE 58: If MXLEN is 64 and U-mode is supported, the UXL field in the mstatus register is a WARL field that encodes the current UXLEN value.
RULE 59: When S-mode is implemented, the set of legal values for the UXL field in the mstatus register excludes any encoding that would cause UXLEN to be greater than SXLEN.
RULE 60: If the XLEN value for any privilege mode, as configured by the corresponding fields in the mstatus register, is less than the widest supported XLEN, then all operations must ignore source operand register bits above the configured XLEN and must sign-extend results to fill the entire widest supported XLEN in the destination register.
RULE 61: If the XLEN for a privilege mode, as defined by the mstatus register, is less than the widest supported XLEN, then PC bits above XLEN are ignored and any write to the PC is sign-extended to fill the widest supported XLEN.
RULE 62: The architecture imposes no checks that lower-privilege XLEN settings, as specified by the mstatus fields, are less than or equal to the XLEN setting of the next-higher privilege mode.
RULE 63: When a HINT instruction executes while the current XLEN setting from the mstatus register is less than MXLEN and the bits MXLEN..XLEN of the destination register are not all equal to bit XLEN-1, it is implementation-defined whether those upper bits are left unchanged or overwritten with copies of bit XLEN-1.
RULE 64: The implementation-defined behavior of upper-bit handling for a HINT instruction is observable only by privilege modes whose XLEN setting, as defined in the mstatus register, is greater than the current XLEN; it is invisible to the current privilege mode.
RULE 65: When the MPRV bit in mstatus is 0, explicit memory accesses behave as normal, using the translation and protection mechanisms of the current privilege mode.
RULE 66: When the MPRV bit in mstatus is 1, load and store memory addresses are translated and protected, and endianness is applied as though the current privilege mode were set to MPP.
RULE 67: Instruction address-translation and protection are unaffected by the setting of the MPRV bit in mstatus.
RULE 68: The MPRV bit in mstatus is read-only 0 if U-mode is not supported.
RULE 69: An MRET or SRET instruction that changes the privilege mode to a mode less privileged than M also sets the MPRV bit in mstatus to 0.
RULE 70: When the MPRV bit in mstatus is 1, load and store memory addresses are treated as though the current XLEN were set to MPP's XLEN, following the rules in Section 3.1.6.3.
RULE 71: When the MXR bit in mstatus is 0, only loads from pages marked readable (R=1) will succeed.
RULE 72: When the MXR bit in mstatus is 1, loads from pages marked either readable or executable (R=1 or X=1) will succeed.
RULE 73: MXR in mstatus has no effect when page-based virtual memory is not in effect.
RULE 74: The MXR bit in mstatus is read-only 0 if S-mode is not supported.
RULE 75: When the SUM bit in mstatus is 0, S-mode memory accesses to pages that are accessible by U-mode (U=1) will fault.
RULE 76: When the SUM bit in mstatus is 1, S-mode memory accesses to pages that are accessible by U-mode are permitted.
RULE 77: SUM in mstatus has no effect when page-based virtual memory is not in effect.
RULE 78: SUM in mstatus is ordinarily ignored when not executing in S-mode, but it is in effect when MPRV=1 and MPP=S.
RULE 79: The SUM bit in mstatus is read-only 0 if S-mode is not supported or if satp.MODE is read-only 0.
RULE 80: The MXR mechanisms encoded in mstatus have no impact on whether access-fault exceptions are raised due to PMAs.
RULE 81: The SUM mechanisms encoded in mstatus have no impact on whether access-fault exceptions are raised due to PMP.
RULE 82: The MBE, SBE, and UBE bits are fields in mstatus and mstatush that control the endianness of memory accesses other than instruction fetches.
RULE 83: Instruction fetches are always little-endian and are not affected by the mstatus MBE, SBE, or UBE bits.
RULE 84: The mstatus.MBE bit controls the endianness of non-instruction-fetch memory accesses made from M-mode when mstatus.MPRV = 0.
RULE 85: When mstatus.MBE = 0, non-instruction-fetch memory accesses from M-mode are little-endian.
RULE 86: When mstatus.MBE = 1, non-instruction-fetch memory accesses from M-mode are big-endian.
RULE 87: If S-mode is not supported, the mstatus.SBE bit is read-only 0.
RULE 88: The mstatus.SBE bit controls the endianness of explicit load and store memory accesses made from S-mode.
RULE 89: When mstatus.SBE = 0, explicit load and store memory accesses from S-mode are little-endian.
RULE 90: When mstatus.SBE = 1, explicit load and store memory accesses from S-mode are big-endian.
RULE 91: If U-mode is not supported, the mstatus.UBE bit is read-only 0.
RULE 92: The mstatus.UBE bit controls the endianness of explicit load and store memory accesses made from U-mode.
RULE 93: When mstatus.UBE = 0, explicit load and store memory accesses from U-mode are little-endian.
RULE 94: When mstatus.UBE = 1, explicit load and store memory accesses from U-mode are big-endian.
RULE 95: The endianness of implicit accesses to supervisor-level memory-management data structures is always controlled by the mstatus.SBE bit.
RULE 96: The TVM field in mstatus is a WARL field.
RULE 97: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to read the satp CSR while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 98: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to write the satp CSR while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 99: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to execute an SFENCE.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 100: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to execute a SINVAL.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 101: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to read or write the satp CSR while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 102: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to execute an SFENCE.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 103: When the TVM bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to execute a SINVAL.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 104: The TVM bit in mstatus is read-only 0 when S-mode is not supported.
RULE 105: The TW field in mstatus is a WARL field.
RULE 106: The TW bit in mstatus is read-only 0 when there are no modes less privileged than M.
RULE 107: The TSR field in mstatus is a WARL field.
RULE 108: When the TSR bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to execute SRET while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 109: When the TSR bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to execute SRET while executing in S-mode are permitted.
RULE 110: The TSR bit in mstatus is read-only 0 when S-mode is not supported.
RULE 111: The mstatus register contains the FS[1:0] and VS[1:0] fields, which are WARL fields, and the XS[1:0] field, which is a read-only field.
RULE 112: The SD bit in mstatus is a read-only bit that summarizes whether either the FS, VS, or XS fields signal the presence of dirty state that will require saving extended user context to memory.
RULE 113: If the FS, VS, and XS fields in mstatus are all read-only zero, then the SD bit in mstatus is also always zero.
RULE 114: If the F extension is implemented, the FS field in mstatus shall not be read-only zero.
RULE 115: If neither the F extension nor S-mode is implemented, then the FS field in mstatus is read-only zero.
RULE 116: If S-mode is implemented but the F extension is not, the FS field in mstatus may optionally be read-only zero.
RULE 117: Implementations with S-mode but without the F extension are permitted, but not required, to make the FS field in mstatus be read-only zero.
RULE 118: If the v registers are implemented, the VS field in mstatus shall not be read-only zero.
RULE 119: If neither the v registers nor S-mode is implemented, then the VS field in mstatus is read-only zero.
RULE 120: If S-mode is implemented but the v registers are not, the VS field in mstatus may optionally be read-only zero.
RULE 121: In harts without additional user extensions requiring new state, the XS field in mstatus is read-only zero.
RULE 122: Changing the setting of the FS field in mstatus has no effect on the contents of the floating-point register state.
RULE 123: Setting the FS field in mstatus to Off does not destroy the floating-point state, and setting the FS field to Initial does not clear the floating-point contents.
RULE 124: Changing the setting of the VS field in mstatus has no effect on the contents of the vector register state.
RULE 125: The FS field in mstatus is set directly by privileged code when resuming a user context, while the XS field in mstatus is set indirectly by writing to the status register of the individual extensions.
RULE 126: Machine mode and Supervisor mode share a single copy of the FS, VS, and XS bits in mstatus.
RULE 127: The SD bit in mstatus is read-only and is set when either the FS, VS, or XS bits in mstatus encode a Dirty state (i.e., SD = (FS==0b11 OR VS==0b11 OR XS==0b11)).
RULE 128: In mstatus, the encoding 0 for FS and VS means Off, 1 means Initial, 2 means Clean, and 3 means Dirty.
RULE 129: In mstatus, the encoding 0 for XS means All off, 1 means None dirty or clean with some on, 2 means None dirty with some clean, and 3 means Some dirty.
RULE 130: When an extension's status field in mstatus is set to Off, any instruction that attempts to read or write the corresponding state causes an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 131: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Off, executing an instruction that reads the corresponding state causes an exception.
RULE 132: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Off, executing an instruction that may modify the corresponding state causes an exception.
RULE 133: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Initial, executing an instruction that may modify the corresponding state causes the field to transition to Dirty.
RULE 134: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Clean, executing an instruction that may modify the corresponding state causes the field to transition to Dirty.
RULE 135: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Dirty, executing an instruction that may modify the corresponding state leaves the field in the Dirty state.
RULE 136: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Off, executing an instruction to unconfigure the unit causes an exception.
RULE 137: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Initial, executing an instruction to unconfigure the unit leaves the field in the Initial state.
RULE 138: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Clean, executing an instruction to unconfigure the unit transitions the field to the Initial state.
RULE 139: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Dirty, executing an instruction to unconfigure the unit transitions the field to the Initial state.
RULE 140: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Off, executing an instruction to disable the unit leaves the field in the Off state.
RULE 141: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Initial, executing an instruction to disable the unit transitions the field to the Off state.
RULE 142: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Clean, executing an instruction to disable the unit transitions the field to the Off state.
RULE 143: If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Dirty, executing an instruction to disable the unit transitions the field to the Off state.
RULE 144: Executing an instruction to enable a unit when the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Off transitions the field to the Initial state.
RULE 145: Executing an instruction to enable a unit when the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Initial leaves the field in the Initial state.
RULE 146: Executing an instruction to enable a unit when the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Clean transitions the field to the Initial state.
RULE 147: Executing an instruction to enable a unit when the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Dirty transitions the field to the Initial state.
RULE 148: Each xPELP field (SPELP or MPELP) in mstatus encodes the value 0 as NO_LP_EXPECTED, meaning no landing pad instruction is expected, and encodes the value 1 as LP_EXPECTED, meaning a landing pad instruction is expected.
RULE 149: When a trap is delegated to S-mode, the SPP field of mstatus is written with the active privilege mode at the time of the trap.
RULE 150: When a trap is delegated to S-mode, the SPIE field of mstatus is written with the value of the SIE field at the time of the trap.
RULE 151: When a trap is delegated to S-mode, the SIE field of mstatus is cleared.
RULE 152: When a trap is delegated to S-mode, the MPP and MPIE fields of mstatus are not written.
RULE 153: If the current privilege mode is M and the MIE bit in mstatus is set, an interrupt i will trap to M-mode, causing the privilege mode to change to M-mode.
RULE 154: If the current privilege mode has less privilege than M-mode, an interrupt i will trap to M-mode, causing the privilege mode to change to M-mode regardless of the MIE bit in mstatus.
RULE 155: After an explicit write to any CSR on which the interrupt-trap conditions expressly depend, including mstatus, the interrupt-trap conditions must be evaluated immediately.
RULE 156: After execution of an xRET instruction, the interrupt-trap conditions, which depend on mstatus, must be evaluated immediately.
RULE 157: If the TSR bit in the mstatus register is 1, execution of the SRET instruction should raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 158: A hart must resume execution when a locally enabled interrupt becomes pending even if the MIE or SIE bits in mstatus are 0.
RULE 159: Implementations should honor individual interrupt enable bits in mstatus such as MTIE and should avoid resuming the hart if an interrupt is pending but its individual enable bit is not set.
RULE 160: Upon reset, the mstatus fields MIE and MPRV are reset to 0.
RULE 161: If little-endian memory accesses are supported, then upon reset the mstatus or mstatush field MBE is reset to 0.
RULE 162: If the MPRV bit in mstatus is set and the MPP field in mstatus contains the value S or U, then PMP checks are applied to data accesses performed while the processor is in M-mode.
RULE 163: When NMIE is 0, the hart behaves as though the MPRV field of mstatus is cleared, regardless of the actual setting of mstatus.MPRV.
RULE 164: If the MNRET instruction changes the privilege mode to a mode less privileged than M, then mstatus.MPRV MUST be set to 0.
RULE 165: The SPP bit in mstatus indicates the privilege level at which a hart was executing before entering supervisor mode.
RULE 166: When a trap is taken, the SPP bit in mstatus is set to 0 if the trap originated from user mode, otherwise it is set to 1.
RULE 167: When an SRET instruction is executed, the privilege level is set to user mode if the SPP bit in mstatus is 0, otherwise to supervisor mode if the SPP bit in mstatus is 1, and then the SPP bit in mstatus is set to 0.
RULE 168: When a trap is taken into supervisor mode, the SPIE bit in mstatus is set to the value of the SIE bit in mstatus, and the SIE bit in mstatus is set to 0.
RULE 169: When an SRET instruction is executed, the SIE bit in mstatus is set to the value of the SPIE bit in mstatus, then the SPIE bit in mstatus is set to 1.
RULE 170: In a straightforward implementation, reading or writing any field in sstatus is equivalent to reading or writing the homonymous field in mstatus.
RULE 171: When the V bit is zero, any access to the SPELP field defined by the Zicfilp extension accesses the homonymous fields of the mstatus register.
RULE 172: The SUM field of the mstatus register is consulted when determining whether a requested memory access is allowed by the pte.u bit.
RULE 173: The MXR field of the mstatus register is consulted when determining whether a requested memory access is allowed by the pte.u bit.
RULE 174: If the decision, which uses the current privilege mode and the SUM and MXR fields of the mstatus register, determines that the access is not allowed, the implementation MUST stop and raise a page-fault exception corresponding to the original access type.
RULE 175: If mstatus.TVM=1, an attempt to execute SINVAL.VMA or HINVAL.GVMA in S-mode or HS-mode raises an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 176: SFENCE.W.INVAL and SFENCE.INVAL.IR are unaffected by the mstatus.TVM field and therefore are always permitted in S-mode and VS-mode.
RULE 177: When mstatus.TVM=1 (or hstatus.VTVM=1), SFENCE.W.INVAL and SFENCE.INVAL.IR instructions do not need to be trapped because they have only ordering effects and no visible side effects.
RULE 178: The mstatus fields TSR, TW, and TVM have corresponding hstatus fields VTSR, VTW, and VTVM that are defined analogously but affect execution only in VS-mode and cause virtual-instruction exceptions instead of illegal-instruction exceptions.
RULE 179: When the TVM field of mstatus equals 1, attempts to read or write hgatp while executing in HS-mode must raise an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 180: When the V field in mstatus is 0, vsstatus does not directly affect the behavior of the machine.
RULE 181: If a virtual-machine load/store instruction (HLV, HLVX, or HSV) is used to execute a load or store as though V=1, then vsstatus can affect the behavior of the machine even when the V field in mstatus is 0.
RULE 182: If the MPRV feature in mstatus is used to execute a load or store as though V=1, then vsstatus can affect the behavior of the machine even when the V field in mstatus is 0.
RULE 183: The MPRV feature in the mstatus register can be used to execute a load or store as though the V bit is 1.
RULE 184: When the V bit is 0, the vsatp register does not directly affect the behavior of the machine unless a virtual-machine load/store or the MPRV feature in the mstatus register is used to execute a load or store as though V is 1.
RULE 185: mstatus.TVM does not cause HFENCE.VVMA to trap.
RULE 186: HFENCE.GVMA is valid only in HS-mode when mstatus.TVM = 0.
RULE 187: HFENCE.GVMA is valid in M-mode irrespective of the value of mstatus.TVM.
RULE 188: Executing HFENCE.GVMA in HS-mode when mstatus.TVM = 1 causes an illegal-instruction exception.
RULE 189: MPV is written by the implementation whenever a trap is taken into M-mode.
RULE 190: When a trap is taken into M-mode, MPV in mstatus is set to the value of the virtualization mode V at the time of the trap.
RULE 191: When an MRET instruction is executed, the virtualization mode V is set to MPV in mstatus unless MPP = 3, in which case V remains 0.
RULE 192: GVA is written by the implementation whenever a trap is taken into M-mode.
RULE 193: For any trap that writes a guest virtual address to mtval, GVA in mstatus is set to 1.
RULE 194: For any other trap into M-mode, GVA in mstatus is set to 0.
RULE 195: The TSR field of mstatus affects execution only in HS-mode and does not affect execution in VS-mode.
RULE 196: The TVM field of mstatus affects execution only in HS-mode and does not affect execution in VS-mode.
RULE 197: The TW field of mstatus affects execution in all modes except M-mode.
RULE 198: Setting TVM = 1 in mstatus prevents HS-mode from accessing hgatp or executing HFENCE.GVMA or HINVAL.GVMA.
RULE 199: Setting TVM = 1 in mstatus has no effect on accesses to vsatp or on execution of HFENCE.VVMA or HINVAL.VVMA.
RULE 200: Setting TVM = 1 in mstatus does not cause traps for accesses to vsatp, for execution of HFENCE.VVMA or HINVAL.VVMA, or for any actions taken in VS-mode.
RULE 201: When MPRV = 0 in mstatus, translation and protection behave as normal.
RULE 202: When MPRV = 1 in mstatus, explicit memory accesses are translated and protected, and endianness is applied as though the current virtualization mode were MPV and the current nominal privilege mode were MPP.
RULE 203: When MPRV = 1, MPV = 0, and MPP = 0 in mstatus, explicit memory accesses are treated as U-level accesses with HS-level translation and protection only.
RULE 204: When MPRV = 1, MPV = 0, and MPP = 1 in mstatus, explicit memory accesses are treated as HS-level accesses with HS-level translation and protection only.
RULE 205: When MPRV = 1 and MPP = 3 in mstatus (MPV value is ignored), explicit memory accesses are treated as M-level accesses with no translation.
RULE 206: When MPRV = 1, MPV = 1, and MPP = 0 in mstatus, explicit memory accesses are treated as VU-level accesses with two-stage translation and protection; the HS-level MXR bit makes any executable page readable, and vsstatus.MXR makes readable those pages marked executable at the VS translation stage only if readable at the guest-physical translation stage.
RULE 207: When MPRV = 1, MPV = 1, and MPP = 1 in mstatus, explicit memory accesses are treated as VS-level accesses with two-stage translation and protection; the HS-level MXR bit makes any executable page readable, vsstatus.MXR makes readable those pages marked executable at the VS translation stage only if readable at the guest-physical translation stage, and vsstatus.SUM applies instead of the HS-level SUM bit.
RULE 208: MPRV in mstatus does not affect the virtual-machine load/store instructions HLV, HLVX, and HSV.
RULE 209: The explicit loads and stores of the HLV, HLVX, and HSV instructions always act as though V = 1 and the nominal privilege mode were hstatus.SPVP, overriding the effect of MPRV in mstatus.
RULE 210: When the V bit in mstatus is 1, a virtual-instruction exception with code 22 is raised instead of an illegal-instruction exception if the attempted instruction is HS-qualified and execution is prevented because of insufficient privilege or because the instruction is expressly disabled by a supervisor or hypervisor CSR such as scounteren or hcounteren.
RULE 211: The TSR and TVM fields of mstatus are ignored when determining exceptions in VS-mode because they are intended to affect only S-mode (HS-mode).
RULE 212: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the virtualization mode bit V in mstatus is set to 0.
RULE 213: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPV field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 0 if the previous privilege mode was U-mode.
RULE 214: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPP field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 0 if the previous privilege mode was U-mode.
RULE 215: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPV field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 0 if the previous privilege mode was HS-mode.
RULE 216: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPP field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 1 if the previous privilege mode was HS-mode.
RULE 217: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPV field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 0 if the previous privilege mode was M-mode.
RULE 218: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPP field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 3 if the previous privilege mode was M-mode.
RULE 219: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPV field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 1 if the previous privilege mode was VU-mode.
RULE 220: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPP field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 0 if the previous privilege mode was VU-mode.
RULE 221: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPV field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 1 if the previous privilege mode was VS-mode.
RULE 222: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the MPP field in mstatus (or mstatush) is set to 1 if the previous privilege mode was VS-mode.
RULE 223: When returning from a trap, the MPV field in mstatus is ignored if the MPP field in mstatus equals 3.
RULE 224: When the MRET instruction is executed, the new privilege mode is determined from the values of the MPP and MPV fields in mstatus or mstatush as specified by the architecture.
RULE 225: When the MRET instruction is executed, the MPV field in mstatus or mstatush is set to 0.
RULE 226: When the MRET instruction is executed, the MPP field in mstatus or mstatush is set to 0.
RULE 227: When the MRET instruction is executed, the MIE field in mstatus or mstatush is written with the current value of the MPIE field.
RULE 228: When the MRET instruction is executed, the MPIE field in mstatus or mstatush is set to 1.
RULE 229: The SPELP bit in mstatus can be accessed through the sstatus CSR.
RULE 230: When a trap is taken into privilege mode x, the x PELP bit in mstatus is set to the current ELP value.
RULE 231: When a trap is taken into privilege mode x, the ELP field in mstatus is set to NO_LP_EXPECTED.
RULE 232: When executing an MRET or SRET instruction and the new privilege mode is y, the ELP field in mstatus is set to the value of the x PELP bit in mstatus if the LPE bit of privilege mode y is 1.
RULE 233: When executing an MRET or SRET instruction and the new privilege mode is y, the ELP field in mstatus is set to NO_LP_EXPECTED if the LPE bit of privilege mode y is 0.
RULE 234: When executing an MRET or SRET instruction, the x PELP bit in mstatus is set to NO_LP_EXPECTED.

REGISTER: mtinst
NUMBER: 0x34a
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=VALUE
EXTENSIONS: H
RULE 1: When a trap occurs, the value written to mtinst is produced by applying the standard transformation defined for cache-block management instructions and cache-block zero instructions.
RULE 2: The operation field used in the standard transformation for mtinst corresponds to the 12 most significant bits of the trapping instruction.
RULE 3: A zero may be written into mtinst instead of the value produced by the standard transformation as defined by the hypervisor extension.
RULE 4: The mtinst CSR resides in the Machine privilege level.
RULE 5: The mtinst CSR has MRW access type, meaning it is machine-read/write.
RULE 6: When a trap is taken into M-mode, mtinst is written with a value.
RULE 7: On a guest-page fault, the mtinst CSR may be written with information about the faulting instruction or other reason for the access.
RULE 8: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the architecture writes the CSR mtinst as part of the trap-entry state update.
RULE 9: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the architecture writes the CSR mtinst together with the CSRs mepc, mcause, mtval, and mtval2.
RULE 10: On any trap into M-mode or HS-mode, hardware automatically writes one of the following values into the mtinst CSR: zero, a transformation of the trapping instruction, a custom value (allowed only if the trapping instruction is non-standard), or a special pseudoinstruction.
RULE 11: Except when a pseudoinstruction value is required, the value written to mtinst may always be zero, indicating that the hardware provides no information for that trap.
RULE 12: On an interrupt, the value written to mtinst is always zero.
RULE 13: On a synchronous exception, if a non-zero value is written to mtinst and bit 0 of mtinst is 1 and setting bit 1 to 1 yields a valid encoding of a standard instruction, then the mtinst value represents a transformation of the trapping instruction.
RULE 14: On a synchronous exception, if a non-zero value is written to mtinst and bit 0 of mtinst is 1 and setting bit 1 to 1 yields an instruction encoding that is explicitly designated for a custom instruction (not an unused reserved encoding), then the mtinst value represents a custom value.
RULE 15: On a synchronous exception, if a non-zero value is written to mtinst, the value is one of the special pseudoinstructions defined later and bits 1:0 of mtinst equal 00, then the mtinst value represents a special pseudoinstruction.
RULE 16: Values with bits 1:0 equal to binary 10 are excluded from being written to mtinst unless a future standard defines additional cases.
RULE 17: Table 55 specifies, for each standard exception cause, which of the four possible mtinst values (zero, transformed standard instruction, custom value, pseudoinstruction value) may be automatically written.
RULE 18: For exceptions that prevent the fetching of an instruction, only zero or a pseudoinstruction value may be written to mtinst.
RULE 19: A custom value may be automatically written to mtinst only if the instruction that traps is non-standard.
RULE 20: If a synchronous trap occurs for a standard instruction for which no transformation has been defined, mtinst shall be written with zero or, under certain circumstances, with a special pseudoinstruction value.
RULE 21: Standard transformations are currently defined only for memory-access instructions (loads, stores, and AMO instructions); consequently, only exception causes that arise from explicit memory accesses may result in a transformed standard instruction being written to mtinst.
RULE 22: Transformed standard load instructions (non-compressed LB, LBU, LH, LHU, LW, LWU, LD, FLW, FLD, FLQ, FLH) have the same funct3, rd, and opcode fields in mtinst as in the trapping load instruction.
RULE 23: Transformed standard store instructions (non-compressed SB, SH, SW, SD, FSW, FSD, FSQ, FSH) have the same rs2, funct3, and opcode fields in mtinst as in the trapping store instruction.
RULE 24: Transformed standard atomic instructions (load-reserved, store-conditional, AMO) have all fields in mtinst the same as the trapping instruction except bits 19:15 (Addr. Offset).
RULE 25: Transformed standard virtual-machine load/store instructions (HLV, HLVX, HSV) have all fields in mtinst the same as the trapping instruction except bits 19:15 (Addr. Offset).
RULE 26: In all transformed instructions, the Addr. Offset field (bits 19:15 of mtinst, replacing the original rs1 field) is the positive difference between the faulting virtual address (written to mtval or stval) and the original virtual address.
RULE 27: The Addr. Offset field in a transformed instruction can be non-zero only for a misaligned memory access.
RULE 28: For basic loads and stores, the transformation replaces the instruction's immediate offset fields with zero in mtinst.
RULE 29: If a guest-page-fault is caused by an implicit memory access for VS-stage address translation and a non-zero value is written to mtval2 or htval, then mtinst must be written with a special pseudoinstruction value taken from Table 56; zero is not allowed.
RULE 30: The special pseudoinstruction encoding 0x00002003 (and 0x00002023) corresponds to the instruction lw x0,0(x0).
RULE 31: The special pseudoinstruction encodings 0x00003003 and 0x00003023 correspond to the instruction sw x0,0(x0).
RULE 32: The special pseudoinstruction encodings 0x00003003 and 0x00003023 also correspond to the 64-bit instructions ld x0,0(x0) and sd x0,0(x0) respectively.
RULE 33: A write pseudoinstruction (0x00002020 or 0x00003020) is used when the machine automatically updates bits A and/or D in VS-level page tables; all other implicit VS-stage accesses are reads.

REGISTER: mtval
NUMBER: 0x343
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=VALUE
EXTENSIONS: H, Smdbltrp, Smrnmi, Zicfilp, Zicfiss
RULE 1: The mtval CSR is machine-read/write (MRW) privileged, meaning it can be read and written when the processor is in machine mode.
RULE 2: When a double trap occurs, the RNMI handler is not provided with the trap's mtval information (nor the mtval2 information).
RULE 3: When a trap is delegated to S-mode, the mtval register is not written.
RULE 4: mtval is an MXLEN-bit read-write register formatted as shown in Figure 23.
RULE 5: When a trap is taken into M-mode, mtval is either set to zero or written with exception-specific information to assist software in handling the trap.
RULE 6: When a trap is not taken into M-mode, mtval is never written by the implementation, though it may be explicitly written by software.
RULE 7: If the hardware platform specifies that no exceptions set mtval to a non-zero value, then mtval is read-only zero.
RULE 8: If mtval is written with a non-zero value when a breakpoint, address-misaligned, access-fault, page-fault, or hardware-error exception occurs on an instruction fetch, load, or store, then mtval will contain the faulting virtual address.
RULE 9: On a breakpoint exception raised by an EBREAK or C.EBREAK instruction, mtval is written with either zero or the virtual address of the instruction.
RULE 10: When page-based virtual memory is enabled, mtval is written with the faulting virtual address even for physical-memory access-fault exceptions.
RULE 11: If mtval is written with a non-zero value when a misaligned load or store causes an access-fault, page-fault, or hardware-error exception, then mtval will contain the virtual address of the portion of the access that caused the fault.
RULE 12: If mtval is written with a non-zero value when an instruction access-fault, page-fault, or hardware-error exception occurs on a hart with variable-length instructions, then mtval will contain the virtual address of the portion of the instruction that caused the fault, while mepc will point to the beginning of the instruction.
RULE 13: If mtval is written with a non-zero value when an illegal-instruction exception occurs, then mtval will contain the shortest of the actual faulting instruction, the first ILEN bits of the faulting instruction, or the first MXLEN bits of the faulting instruction.
RULE 14: The value loaded into mtval on an illegal-instruction exception is right-justified and all unused upper bits are cleared to zero.
RULE 15: The entire instruction (or at least the first MXLEN bits) must be fetched into mtval before taking the trap.
RULE 16: On a trap caused by a software-check exception, mtval holds the cause for the exception with the defined encodings 0 for no information provided, 2 for Landing Pad Fault, and 3 for Shadow Stack Fault.
RULE 17: For other traps, mtval is set to zero, but a future standard may redefine mtval's setting for other traps.
RULE 18: If mtval is not read-only zero, it is a WARL register that must be able to hold all valid virtual addresses and the value zero.
RULE 19: Prior to writing mtval, implementations may convert an invalid address into some other invalid address that mtval is capable of holding.
RULE 20: If the feature to return the faulting instruction bits is implemented, mtval must also be able to hold all values less than 2^N, where N is the smaller of MXLEN and ILEN.
RULE 21: The CSR mtval must not be a read-only zero register.
RULE 22: The GVA field of mtval is written by the implementation whenever a trap is taken into M-mode.
RULE 23: When a breakpoint, address-misaligned, access-fault, page-fault, or guest-page-fault trap writes a guest virtual address to mtval, the GVA field of mtval is set to 1.
RULE 24: For any trap into M-mode that does not write a guest virtual address to mtval, the GVA field of mtval is set to 0.
RULE 25: On breakpoint, address-misaligned, access-fault, page-fault, or guest-page-fault traps, mtval is written with the guest virtual address that caused the trap.
RULE 26: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the mtval CSR is written with exception-specific information and mtval2 is also written.
RULE 27: For misaligned load or store operations that cause a guest-page-fault, mtval contains the virtual address of the faulting portion of the access.
RULE 28: For instruction guest-page faults on systems that support variable-length instructions, mtval contains the virtual address of the faulting portion of the instruction.
RULE 29: On a guest-page fault, the mtval CSR is written with the faulting guest virtual address, which is the same value that would be written for a regular page fault.
RULE 30: When an instruction fetch or a misaligned memory access straddles a page boundary and a guest-page fault occurs, the faulting virtual address written to mtval is the same as would be required for a regular page fault.
RULE 31: When an instruction fetch or a misaligned memory access straddles a page boundary and a guest-page fault occurs, the faulting virtual address written to mtval may be a page-boundary address that is higher than the instruction's original virtual address if the byte at that page boundary is among the accessed bytes.
RULE 32: When a guest-page fault is not due to an implicit memory access for VS-stage address translation, a nonzero guest physical address written to mtval2 shall correspond to the exact virtual address written to mtval.
RULE 33: When a virtual-instruction trap occurs, the mtval register is written in the same manner as it is for an illegal-instruction trap.
RULE 34: When a trap is taken into M-mode, the implementation writes the CSR mtval (together with mepc, mcause, mtval2, and mtinst).

REGISTER: mtvec
NUMBER: 0x305
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..2=BASE, 1..0=MODE
EXTENSIONS: -
RULE 1: The mtvec register is a Machine-mode CSR that is both readable and writable (MRW).
RULE 2: The mtvec register is an MXLEN-bit WARL read/write register that holds trap-vector configuration composed of a vector base address (BASE) and a vector mode (MODE).
RULE 3: The mtvec register must always be implemented.
RULE 4: The value in the BASE field of mtvec must always be aligned on a 4-byte boundary.
RULE 5: When the BASE field of mtvec is used as an address, the lower two bits are filled with zeroes to obtain an XLEN-bit address that is always aligned on a 4-byte boundary.
RULE 6: A mtvec MODE field value of 0 is named Direct and specifies that all traps set the pc to BASE.
RULE 7: A mtvec MODE field value of 2 or greater is reserved.
RULE 8: When mtvec MODE = Direct, all traps into machine mode cause the pc to be set to the address in the BASE field.
RULE 9: When mtvec MODE = Vectored, all synchronous exceptions into machine mode cause the pc to be set to the address in the BASE field.
RULE 10: For a machine-mode timer interrupt with interrupt cause 2, mtvec causes the pc to be set to BASE + 0x1c (i.e., BASE + 4 × 2 + 4-byte offset for the cause field).

REGISTER: mvendorid
NUMBER: 0xf11
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: 32
FIELDS: 31..7=Bank, 6..0=Offset
EXTENSIONS: -
RULE 1: The mvendorid CSR has Machine Read-Only (MRO) privilege.
RULE 2: The mvendorid register must be readable in any implementation.
RULE 3: The mvendorid register can return the value 0 to indicate the field is not implemented or that the implementation is non-commercial.
RULE 4: The mvendorid register encodes the number of one-byte continuation codes in its Bank field.
RULE 5: The mvendorid register encodes the final byte of the JEDEC manufacturer ID in its Offset field, discarding the parity bit.
RULE 6: The Bank field of the mvendorid register encodes a value that is one less than the JEDEC bank number.

REGISTER: mvien
NUMBER: 0x308
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: 64
FIELDS: 63..14=WPRI, 13..13=LCOFI, 12..0=WPRI
EXTENSIONS: Smaia, Smcdeleg, Ssaia, Sscofpmf
RULE 1: In implementations that support Smcdeleg, Sscofpmf, and Smaia, the local-counter-overflow interrupt (LCOFI) bit (bit 13) in CSR mvien is implemented.
RULE 2: In implementations that support Smcdeleg, Sscofpmf, and Smaia, the local-counter-overflow interrupt (LCOFI) bit (bit 13) in CSR mvien is writable.

REGISTER: mvip
NUMBER: 0x309
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: 64
FIELDS: 63..14=WPRI, 13..13=LCOFI, 12..0=WPRI
EXTENSIONS: Smaia, Ssaia
RULE 1: For implementations that support Smcdeleg, Sscofpmf, and Smaia, the local-counter-overflow interrupt (LCOFI) bit (bit 13) is implemented in the CSR mvip.
RULE 2: For implementations that support Smcdeleg, Sscofpmf, and Smaia, the local-counter-overflow interrupt (LCOFI) bit (bit 13) is writable in the CSR mvip.

REGISTER: pmpaddr0
NUMBER: 0x3b0
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: Smepmp
RULE 1: pmpaddr0[G-1] may have an underlying value of 1 while a read of pmpaddr0[G-1] returns 0.
RULE 2: Executing CSRRC or CSRRS to modify a different bit will cause 0 to be read from pmpaddr0[G-1] and then written back, updating the underlying value to 0.
RULE 3: pmpaddr0 has machine-mode read/write (MRW) privilege.
RULE 4: In RV64, pmpaddr0 encodes bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address.
RULE 5: pmpaddr0 is a WARL register because not all physical address bits may be implemented.
RULE 6: pmpaddr0 may be read-only zero, as all PMP CSR fields are WARL and may be read-only zero.
RULE 7: pmpaddr0 is only accessible to M-mode.
RULE 8: pmpaddr0 exists only if at least one PMP entry is implemented.
RULE 9: If the PMP entry 0 configuration field A is set to TOR, the lower bound is zero and the entry matches any address y that is less than pmpaddr0.
RULE 10: If pmpaddr0 is zero and the PMP entry 0 configuration field A is TOR, then PMP entry 0 matches no addresses.
RULE 11: In NAPOT mode, the low-order bits of pmpaddr0 encode the size of the matched range according to the pattern of trailing zeros and ones defined in Table 24.
RULE 12: When the PMP granularity G is at least 2 and the configuration field pmpcfg0.A[1] is set (indicating NAPOT mode), the bits pmpaddr0[G-2:0] read as all ones.
RULE 13: When the PMP granularity G is at least 1 and the configuration field pmpcfg0.A[1] is clear (indicating OFF or TOR mode), the bits pmpaddr0[G-1:0] read as all zeros.
RULE 14: The bits pmpaddr0[G-1:0] do not affect the address-matching logic when the entry operates in TOR mode.
RULE 15: Changing the configuration field pmpcfg0.A[1] changes the value read from pmpaddr0 but does not change the underlying stored value, and consequently pmpaddr0[G-1] retains its original value when the entry is switched from NAPOT to TOR/OFF and back to NAPOT.
RULE 16: Software may determine the PMP granularity by writing zero to pmp0cfg, writing all ones to pmpaddr0, reading back pmpaddr0, and interpreting the index G of the least-significant set bit such that the granularity equals 2^G + 2 bytes.
RULE 17: If PMP entry 0 is locked, any write to pmpaddr0 is ignored.
RULE 18: The lock on PMP entry 0 causes the associated address register pmpaddr0 to be ignored.
RULE 19: If PMP entry 1 is locked and pmp1 cfg.A is set to TOR, any write to pmpaddr0 is ignored.
RULE 20: Setting the L bit of PMP entry 0 locks the entry even when its A field is OFF, and consequently any write to pmpaddr0 is ignored.
RULE 21: For the PMP entry containing pmpaddr0 to be valid, the A field of the associated pmpcfg0 register MUST NOT be OFF.
RULE 22: If the address-matching mode A of pmpcfg0 is TOR, then pmpaddr-1 MUST be less than pmpaddr0.
RULE 23: If the address-matching mode A of pmpcfg1 is TOR, then pmpaddr0 MUST be less than pmpaddr1.

REGISTER: pmpaddr1
NUMBER: 0x3b1
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: P, Smepmp
RULE 1: pmpaddr1[G-1] may have an underlying value of 1 while a read of that bit returns 0.
RULE 2: If a CSRRC or CSRRS instruction targets any bit of pmpaddr1 other than the G-1 bit, the operation will read the G-1 bit as 0 and then write that 0 back, causing the underlying G-1 bit value to become 0.
RULE 3: pmpaddr1 has machine-mode read-write (MRW) privilege/visibility.
RULE 4: In RV64 implementations, pmpaddr1 encodes bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address.
RULE 5: pmpaddr1 is a WARL register because not all physical address bits may be implemented.
RULE 6: pmpaddr1 may be read-only zero.
RULE 7: Some PMP settings additionally use the address register of the preceding PMP entry, and when such a setting applies to PMP entry 2, the value stored in pmpaddr1 directly determines the address used for that PMP entry.
RULE 8: If pmpcfg1.A = NA4, then a value of the form yyyy…yyyy in pmpaddr1 encodes a 4-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 9: If pmpcfg1.A = NAPOT and pmpaddr1 has the form yyyy…yyy0, then it encodes an 8-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 10: If pmpcfg1.A = NAPOT and pmpaddr1 has the form yyyy…yy01, then it encodes a 16-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 11: If pmpcfg1.A = NAPOT and pmpaddr1 has the form yyyy…y011, then it encodes a 32-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 12: If pmpcfg1.A = NAPOT and pmpaddr1 has the form yy01…1111, then it encodes a 2 XLEN-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 13: If pmpcfg1.A = NAPOT and pmpaddr1 has the form y011…1111, then it encodes a 2 XLEN+1-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 14: If pmpcfg1.A = NAPOT and pmpaddr1 has the form 0111…1111, then it encodes a 2 XLEN+2-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 15: If pmpcfg1.A = NAPOT and pmpaddr1 has the form 1111…1111, then it encodes a 2 XLEN+3-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 16: If pmpcfg1.A = TOR, then pmpaddr1 forms the top of the address range and the entry matches any address y such that pmpaddr0 ≤ y < pmpaddr1 irrespective of the value of pmpcfg0.A.
RULE 17: If pmpcfg1.A = TOR and pmpaddr0 ≥ pmpaddr1, then PMP entry 1 matches no addresses.
RULE 18: When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg1.A[1] is set, then bits pmpaddr1[G-2:0] read as all ones.
RULE 19: When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg1.A[1] is clear, then bits pmpaddr1[G-1:0] read as all zeros.
RULE 20: Bits pmpaddr1[G-1:0] do not affect the TOR address-matching logic.
RULE 21: Changing pmpcfg1.A[1] affects the value read from pmpaddr1 but does not affect the underlying stored value in pmpaddr1; in particular pmpaddr1[G-1] retains its original value when pmpcfg1.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF then back to NAPOT.
RULE 22: When G ≥ 1, the NA4 mode is not selectable; therefore pmpaddr1 cannot be used in NA4 mode when G ≥ 1.
RULE 23: If PMP entry 1 is locked, writes to pmpaddr1 are ignored.
RULE 24: When the L bit in pmp1cfg is set, PMP entry 1 is considered locked, causing writes to pmpaddr1 to be ignored.
RULE 25: If pmpcfg1.A is TOR, then pmpaddr1 MUST be greater than pmpaddr0.

REGISTER: pmpaddr10
NUMBER: 0x3ba
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: Smepmp
RULE 1: The pmpaddr10 register contains a field pmpaddr10[G-1] that may have an underlying value of 1 while reads of that field return 0.
RULE 2: CSRRS and CSRRC instructions executed on pmpaddr10 may modify bits whose read value differs from their underlying value, even if the corresponding bit in rs1 is not set, and this behavior applies to the pmpaddr10[G-1] field.
RULE 3: Executing a CSRRC or CSRRS instruction on pmpaddr10 to modify a bit other than pmpaddr10[G-1] will cause a read of 0 from pmpaddr10[G-1] and will write back that 0, updating the underlying value of pmpaddr10[G-1] to 0.
RULE 4: pmpaddr10 has Machine-level Read/Write (MRW) privilege.
RULE 5: pmpaddr10 is a WARL (write-any-legal-value-read-legal) field.
RULE 6: pmpaddr10 may read back as zero regardless of the value that was written.
RULE 7: The set of physical-address bits that pmpaddr10 can represent is implementation-dependent because not all physical address bits may be implemented, and any unimplemented bits are treated as WARL.
RULE 8: For pmpaddr10, when it is used for a NAPOT entry, the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 encode the size of the NAPOT range.
RULE 9: If pmpaddr10 matches the pattern yyyy…yyyy and pmpcfg10.A indicates NA4, then the NAPOT range size is 4 bytes.
RULE 10: If the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 match the pattern yyyy…yyy0 and pmpcfg10.A indicates NAPOT, then the NAPOT range size is 8 bytes.
RULE 11: If the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 match the pattern yyyy…yy01 and pmpcfg10.A indicates NAPOT, then the NAPOT range size is 16 bytes.
RULE 12: If the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 match the pattern yyyy…y011 and pmpcfg10.A indicates NAPOT, then the NAPOT range size is 32 bytes.
RULE 13: If the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 match the pattern yy01…1111 and pmpcfg10.A indicates NAPOT, then the NAPOT range size is 2 XLEN bytes.
RULE 14: If the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 match the pattern y011…1111 and pmpcfg10.A indicates NAPOT, then the NAPOT range size is 2 XLEN+1 bytes.
RULE 15: If the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 match the pattern 0111…1111 and pmpcfg10.A indicates NAPOT, then the NAPOT range size is 2 XLEN+2 bytes.
RULE 16: If the low-order bits of pmpaddr10 match the pattern 1111…1111 and pmpcfg10.A indicates NAPOT, then the NAPOT range size is 2 XLEN+3 bytes.
RULE 17: When pmpcfg10.A is TOR, pmpaddr10 defines the top address of the TOR range and pmpaddr9 defines the bottom address of that range.
RULE 18: When pmpcfg10.A is TOR, the entry matches any address y such that pmpaddr9 ≤ y < pmpaddr10, regardless of the value of pmpcfg9.
RULE 19: If pmpaddr9 ≥ pmpaddr10 and pmpcfg10.A is TOR, then entry 10 matches no addresses.
RULE 20: When the granularity G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg10.A[1] is set (NAPOT mode), bits pmpaddr10[G-2:0] read as all ones.
RULE 21: When the granularity G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg10.A[1] is clear (OFF or TOR mode), bits pmpaddr10[G-1:0] read as all zeros.
RULE 22: Bits pmpaddr10[G-1:0] do not affect the TOR address-matching logic.
RULE 23: Changing pmpcfg10.A[1] alters the value read from pmpaddr10 but does not change the underlying stored value of pmpaddr10; specifically, pmpaddr10[G-1] retains its original value when pmpcfg10.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF and then back to NAPOT.
RULE 24: If the L bit of PMP entry 10 is set, writes to pmpaddr10 are ignored.
RULE 25: The lock on PMP entry 10, which causes writes to pmpaddr10 to be ignored, remains in effect until the hart is reset.
RULE 26: Setting the L bit of PMP entry 10 locks the PMP entry, causing writes to pmpaddr10 to be ignored, even when the A field of that entry is set to OFF.
RULE 27: A PMP rule that includes pmpaddr10 must have pmpcfg10.A not equal to OFF.
RULE 28: If pmpcfg10.A is TOR, then pmpaddr9 must be less than pmpaddr10.
RULE 29: During a PMP reset, pmpaddr10 must be re-initialized to a safe default value.

REGISTER: pmpaddr11
NUMBER: 0x3bb
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: Smepmp
RULE 1: A CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that accesses pmpaddr11 may read the bit pmpaddr11[G-1] as 0 even when the underlying value of pmpaddr11[G-1] is 1.
RULE 2: If a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction accesses pmpaddr11 and reads pmpaddr11[G-1] as 0 while the underlying value of pmpaddr11[G-1] is 1, then executing a CSRRC or CSRRS instruction that modifies a different bit must read 0 from pmpaddr11[G-1] and write that 0 back, updating the underlying value of pmpaddr11[G-1] to 0.
RULE 3: pmpaddr11 is a machine-level CSR that is readable and writable.
RULE 4: The pmpaddr registers, including pmpaddr11, are WARL because not all physical address bits may be implemented.
RULE 5: pmpaddr11 may be read-only zero.
RULE 6: For PMP entry 12, address matching may depend on the contents of pmpaddr11 in addition to the address register of entry 12 itself.
RULE 7: If the L bit of PMP entry 11 is set, writes to the pmpaddr11 register are ignored.
RULE 8: Once the L bit of PMP entry 11 has been set, the lock on pmpaddr11 persists for the lifetime of the hart unless a hart reset occurs.
RULE 9: When the L bit of PMP entry 11 is set while its A field is OFF, writes to the pmpaddr11 register are still ignored.
RULE 10: The register pmpaddr11, together with pmpcfg11, encodes a protected physical memory region only when pmpcfg11.A is not OFF.
RULE 11: If pmpcfg11.A is TOR, the architectural constraint requires that the value in pmpaddr10 be less than the value in pmpaddr11.
RULE 12: In TOR mode, pmpaddr11 defines the upper bound address of the protected memory region.

REGISTER: pmpaddr12
NUMBER: 0x3bc
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: P, Smepmp
RULE 1: The CSR pmpaddr12 can be read or written only when the hart is executing in machine mode (M-mode).
RULE 2: The width of the CSR pmpaddr12 equals the architectural register width MXLEN bits.
RULE 3: When the implementation supports RV64, the CSR pmpaddr12 holds bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address associated with PMP entry 12.
RULE 4: The field value of pmpaddr12 is Write-Any-Read-Legal (WARL); any value written that conforms to the implementation's supported address bits is legal, and the implementation may force reads of pmpaddr12 to return zero.
RULE 5: When pmpcfg12.A selects NAPOT (or NA4), the low-order bits of pmpaddr12 determine the match type and size of the region.
RULE 6: When pmpcfg12.A = TOR, pmpaddr12 forms the top of the address range and pmpaddr11 forms the bottom, and the entry matches any address y such that pmpaddr11 ≤ y < pmpaddr12 irrespective of pmpcfg11.
RULE 7: If pmpcfg12.A = TOR and pmpaddr11 ≥ pmpaddr12, then PMP entry 12 matches no addresses.
RULE 8: When G ≥ 2 and pmpcfg12.A[1] = 1 (NAPOT mode), bits pmpaddr12[G-2:0] read back as all ones.
RULE 9: When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg12.A[1] = 0 (OFF or TOR mode), bits pmpaddr12[G-1:0] read back as all zeros.
RULE 10: When G ≥ 1 and pmpcfg12.A[1] = 0 (OFF or TOR mode), bits pmpaddr12[G-1:0] do not affect TOR address-matching logic.
RULE 11: Changing pmpcfg12.A[1] between NAPOT and OFF/TOR does not change the hardware-stored bit pmpaddr12[G-1]; only the read-masked view changes.
RULE 12: If PMP entry 12 is locked, any write to pmpaddr12 is ignored.
RULE 13: Once PMP entry 12 becomes locked, it remains locked until the hart is reset.
RULE 14: Setting the L bit for PMP entry 12 locks the entry, and therefore locks pmpaddr12, even when the A field is set to OFF.

REGISTER: pmpaddr13
NUMBER: 0x3bd
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: P, Smepmp
RULE 1: pmpaddr13 is a machine-level CSR that can be read and written by machine mode (privilege field MRW).
RULE 2: In RV64 implementations, pmpaddr13 encodes bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address.
RULE 3: The register pmpaddr13 is a WARL (write-any-value-read-legal) register.
RULE 4: The register pmpaddr13 may be read-only zero.
RULE 5: Reads of pmpaddr13 must occur in M-mode; reads from lower privilege modes are not permitted.
RULE 6: Writes to pmpaddr13 must occur in M-mode; writes from lower privilege modes are not permitted.
RULE 7: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern of all ones (yyyy…yyyy) together with pmpcfg13.A = NA4 encodes a 4-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 8: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern ending with a single zero (yyyy…yyy0) together with pmpcfg13.A = NAPOT encodes an 8-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 9: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern ending with "01" (yyyy…yy01) together with pmpcfg13.A = NAPOT encodes a 16-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 10: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern ending with "011" (yyyy…y011) together with pmpcfg13.A = NAPOT encodes a 32-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 11: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern of the form "yy01…1111" together with pmpcfg13.A = NAPOT encodes a 2·XLEN-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 12: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern of the form "y011…1111" together with pmpcfg13.A = NAPOT encodes a (2·XLEN+1)-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 13: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern of the form "0111…1111" together with pmpcfg13.A = NAPOT encodes a (2·XLEN+2)-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 14: For pmpaddr13, a bit pattern of the form "1111…1111" together with pmpcfg13.A = NAPOT encodes a (2·XLEN+3)-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 15: If pmpcfg13.A = TOR then pmpaddr13 specifies the top bound of the address range for PMP entry 13.

RULE 12: When pmpcfg21.A selects NAPOT and the three lowest bits of pmpaddr21 are 011 (pattern yyyy…y011), the entry encodes a 32-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 13: When pmpcfg21.A selects NAPOT and the high bits of pmpaddr21 follow the pattern yy01…1111, the entry encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN bytes.
RULE 14: When pmpcfg21.A selects NAPOT and the high bits of pmpaddr21 follow the pattern y011…1111, the entry encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN + 1 bytes.
RULE 15: When pmpcfg21.A selects NAPOT and the high bits of pmpaddr21 follow the pattern 0111…1111, the entry encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN + 2 bytes.
RULE 16: When pmpcfg21.A selects NAPOT and the high bits of pmpaddr21 follow the pattern 1111…1111, the entry encodes a NAPOT range of size 2 × XLEN + 3 bytes.
RULE 17: If pmpcfg21.A = TOR, then entry 21 matches any address y such that pmpaddr20 ≤ y < pmpaddr21, regardless of pmpcfg20.
RULE 18: If pmpcfg21.A = TOR and pmpaddr20 ≥ pmpaddr21, then entry 21 matches no addresses.
RULE 19: When the granularity G is at least 2 and pmpcfg21.A[1] is set (NAPOT mode), the bits pmpaddr21[G-2:0] read as all ones.
RULE 20: When the granularity G is at least 1 and pmpcfg21.A[1] is clear (OFF or TOR mode), the bits pmpaddr21[G-1:0] read as all zeros.
RULE 21: The bits pmpaddr21[G-1:0] do not affect the TOR address-matching logic for entry 21.
RULE 22: Changing pmpcfg21.A[1] alters the value read from pmpaddr21 but does not change the stored bits pmpaddr21[G-1]; thus pmpaddr21[G-1] retains its original value when the mode is changed from NAPOT to TOR/OFF and back to NAPOT.
RULE 23: If the L bit of PMP entry 21 is set (i.e., PMP entry 21 is locked), writes to the pmpaddr21 register are ignored.
RULE 24: A PMP rule that includes pmpaddr21 is considered valid only when the address-matching field A of the associated pmpcfg21 register is not OFF.
RULE 25: When the address-matching field A of the associated pmpcfg21 register is TOR, the PMP rule requires that the value of pmpaddr20 be less than the value of pmpaddr21.

REGISTER: pmpaddr22
NUMBER: 0x3c6
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: Smepmp
RULE 1: The bit pmpaddr22[G-1] may have an underlying value of 1 but is read as 0.
RULE 2: If a CSRRC or CSRRS instruction modifies any bit other than pmpaddr22[G-1], it will cause a read of 0 from pmpaddr22[G-1] and then a write of that 0 back, updating the underlying value of pmpaddr22[G-1] to 0.
RULE 3: pmpaddr22 has privilege MRW (machine-read/write).
RULE 4: pmpaddr22 may be accessed only when the hart is in machine mode.
RULE 5: The value held in pmpaddr22 is a WARL field and may read as zero.
RULE 6: In RV64 implementations, pmpaddr22 encodes bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address for PMP entry 22.
RULE 7: Writes to pmpaddr22 are ignored when PMP entry 22 is locked.
RULE 8: Writes to pmpaddr22 are ignored when PMP entry 23 is locked and its cfg.A field is TOR.
RULE 9: Setting the L bit of PMP entry 22 locks that entry regardless of the value of its A field.
RULE 10: Once PMP entry 22 is locked, it remains locked until a hart reset.
RULE 11: When the L bit of PMP entry 22 is set, R/W/X permissions are enforced for all privilege modes for accesses that match pmpaddr22.
RULE 12: When the L bit of PMP entry 22 is clear, any M-mode access that matches pmpaddr22 succeeds, and the R/W/X permissions apply only to S and U modes.
RULE 13: If the address-matching mode field A of pmpcfg22 is TOR, then the value in pmpaddr21 must be less than the value in pmpaddr22.

REGISTER: pmpaddr23
NUMBER: 0x3c7
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: P, Smepmp
RULE 1: If any bit of pmpaddr23 reads as a different value than its underlying stored value, a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that targets a different bit may still modify that bit.
RULE 2: The most-significant address bit of pmpaddr23 (pmpaddr23[G-1]) may have an underlying stored value of 1 while a read of the CSR returns 0.
RULE 3: When a CSRRC or CSRRS instruction modifies any bit of pmpaddr23 other than pmpaddr23[G-1], the hardware will read pmpaddr23[G-1] as 0 and write that 0 back, thereby changing the underlying stored value of pmpaddr23[G-1] to 0.
RULE 4: If rs1 = x0 in a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that addresses pmpaddr23, the instruction shall not write to pmpaddr23, shall not cause any write-side effects, and shall not raise illegal-instruction exceptions on read-only accesses.
RULE 5: Any CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that specifies pmpaddr23 as the target CSR reads pmpaddr23 and causes any read-side effects of pmpaddr23 regardless of the values in rs1 or rd.
RULE 6: When rs1 = x0 in a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that addresses pmpaddr23, the instruction reads pmpaddr23 and does not write to it.
RULE 7: When rs1 ≠ x0 in a CSRRS or CSRRC instruction that addresses pmpaddr23, the instruction reads pmpaddr23 and writes to it.
RULE 8: pmpaddr23 is a Machine-Read/Write (MRW) control and status register.
RULE 9: For RV64 implementations, pmpaddr23 encodes bits 55 down to 2 of a 56-bit physical address.
RULE 10: pmpaddr23 is a WARL register.
RULE 11: The fields of pmpaddr23 are WARL and may be read-only zero.
RULE 12: pmpaddr23 is accessible only in M-mode.
RULE 13: The address value in pmpaddr23 may be used by PMP entry 24.
RULE 14: When pmpcfg23.A selects NA4, pmpaddr23 encodes a 4-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 15: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low-order bit of pmpaddr23 is 0, pmpaddr23 encodes an 8-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 16: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low-order bits of pmpaddr23 are 01, pmpaddr23 encodes a 16-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 17: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low-order bits of pmpaddr23 are 011, pmpaddr23 encodes a 32-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 18: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low-order bits of pmpaddr23 match the pattern yy01 followed by all ones, pmpaddr23 encodes a 2 XLEN-byte NAPOT range.

RULE 20: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low-order bits of pmpaddr23 match the pattern 0111 followed by all ones, pmpaddr23 encodes a 2 XLEN+2-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 21: When pmpcfg23.A selects NAPOT and the low-order bits of pmpaddr23 are all ones, pmpaddr23 encodes a 2 XLEN+3-byte NAPOT range.
RULE 22: When pmpcfg23.A selects TOR, pmpaddr23 provides the top address of the range while pmpaddr22 provides the bottom address of the range.
RULE 23: When pmpcfg23.A selects TOR, entry 23 matches any address y such that pmpaddr22 ≤ y < pmpaddr23.
RULE 24: If pmpaddr22 ≥ pmpaddr23 and pmpcfg23.A selects TOR, then entry 23 matches no addresses.

RULE 26: When the granularity G is at least 1 and pmpcfg23.A[1] is clear (indicating OFF or TOR mode), bits pmpaddr23[G-1:0] read as all zeros.
RULE 27: Bits pmpaddr23[G-1:0] do not affect the TOR address-matching logic.
RULE 28: Changing pmpcfg23.A[1] changes the value read from pmpaddr23 but does not modify the underlying stored value of pmpaddr23; consequently, pmpaddr23[G-1] retains its original value when pmpcfg23.A is changed from NAPOT to TOR or OFF and then back to NAPOT.
RULE 29: If the L bit in pmp23cfg is set, implementations MUST ignore all writes to pmpaddr23.
RULE 30: When the L bit in pmp23cfg is set, the PMP entry 23 is locked even if pmp23cfg.A is OFF, and implementations MUST ignore writes to pmpaddr23 regardless of the value of pmp23cfg.A.

REGISTER: pmpaddr24
NUMBER: 0x3c8
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN
FIELDS: 63..0=ADDR
EXTENSIONS: Smepmp
RULE 1: pmpaddr24 belongs to the Machine Memory Protection CSR group and has machine-mode read/write (MRW) privilege.
RULE 2: In RV64, pmpaddr24 encodes bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address for PMP entry 24.
RULE 3: pmpaddr24 is a WARL field, so the value written to it may be any value legal for the implemented subset of address bits and may read back as zero.

REGISTER: pmpaddr26
NUMBER: 0x3ca
MODE: M-mode
WIDTH: MXLEN

EXTENSIONS: Smepmp
RULE 1: pmpaddr26[G-1] may have an underlying value of 1 while a read of the register returns 0.

RULE 4: For RV64, pmpaddr26 encodes bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address.

RULE 6: On RV64, pmpaddr26 is limited to bits 55-2 of a 56-bit physical address because the RV64 PMP address registers impose the same limit as the Sv39 and Sv48 virtual-memory schemes.
RULE 7: If the A field of the configuration register associated with pmpaddr26 is 0, then the PMP entry is disabled and matches no addresses.

RULE 11: If the A field of the configuration register associated with pmpaddr26 selects NAPOT and the three least-significant bits of pmpaddr26 are 011, then the entry matches a 32-byte NAPOT range.

RULE 19: When G ≥ 1 and the A field of the configuration register associated with pmpaddr26 has its high bit clear (mode OFF or TOR), then bits pmpaddr26[G-1:0] read as all zeros.
